zh:
“三军得胜回朝，入城叩见天子，车驾避退！”
长安街上，旌旗蔽天，四皇子高坐赤色战马，战甲锃锃，意气风发，当真不愧皇朝第一少年将军之名。此行前来皇都，为皇帝奉上捷报，亦为三军请赏。
正当车马将入皇都，一队旌旗遥遥亦入眼帘。定睛一看，竟是当朝太子车驾。四皇子微微皱眉，早听闻皇帝陛下对边军有疑，此番遣太子车驾与其争道，难道是为削边军之封赏？边军浴血而战，死伤无数，方得此大捷，若他此行让了太子车驾，求不来与大捷相配的封赏，他有何颜面再回边关？心下想定，他冷冷嘱咐车马官道：“不必退让，径自入城。”
华盖之下，太子亦心中惊疑。自己太子之位本已摇摇欲坠，今日不知遭何人设计，此时入城竟正好撞四皇子之车驾。若让四皇子之车驾，其在皇子之间威望更弱是轻，皇帝陛下对边军更加生疑，才是皇朝之大祸。
“切往前走，暂莫退之。”
长安街上，一蒙面女子正眺望城外，正是当朝公主李清韵。听闻此番四皇兄回京，她自然须得第一个迎接。正在街旁等待之时，近卫来告：“太子与四皇子之车驾将相遇于城门，双方皆不肯退让，恐将生祸事！”
李清韵皱眉思忖，当即便道：“速速赶我车驾来！”
大街之上，只见公主车驾疾驰城外。至边军行伍之前，兵士皆惊，列阵以待。公主翻身上车驾之上，前锋大将见来人身影，抚掌大笑：“飞将军来矣！让开队列！”
四皇子纵马而出，亦大笑相迎。原来公主曾女扮男身，悄悄藏于四皇子之行伍，及至沙场方为四皇子所觉。二人并肩驰骋沙场，杀敌无数，兄妹之情更牢不可催。四皇子之亲卫皆识公主，公主骑射皆精，奈何常不识方向，于敌军阵中胡乱冲杀，于是被笑称“飞将军”矣。
兄妹战友重逢，自是喜事，不多赘述。只说公主得知边军车驾不可退之缘由，思忖一番，干脆将四皇子拉至自己车驾之上。
“边军自有苦楚，如今二皇兄处境亦艰难。四皇兄若信我，便上我之车驾，我载两位皇兄，共入皇城！”
“这皇城之中，若皇妹都信不得，我便无人可信了！”
车驾疾驰，至太子驾前。却说那太子亲卫之中，竟有一奸邪之徒。见四皇子与公主齐至，知今日之事不可成，恶胆骤起，竟张弓射箭，直射四皇子面门！
四皇子久经战阵，如何会怕，将那箭矢一把攥住，顿时满身杀气。

奸邪之徒还要再射，太子大惊，斥左右近卫立斩之。公主顿觉不妙，望向四皇子。谁知四皇子只将她护住，全无半点生疑。
“太子之争，已止于此？清韵，若皇城之中待不痛快，随时可随皇兄回边关去。”
太子已知理亏，速下车驾，行礼于四皇子：“御下不严，罪在吾身！只望四弟相信，此绝非吾意！”
四皇子半点不看太子，只望向身侧公主。公主微微颔首，四皇子这才点头：“吾非信你，信吾皇妹矣。”
当日长安城中有奇闻，公主竟与太子共迎四皇子边军车驾，三人坐公主车驾一同入城，兄妹情深，成一佳话。
三人却不知，此时后宫那新晋皇后已是雷霆震怒。五皇子年幼，这前面四位皇子不争斗起来，她如何能有机会？
却说公主府中，三皇子正好整以暇，待公主回府。李清韵甫一进门，那在朝堂之上叱咤风云，威风八面的三皇子便现了原形，四仰八叉躺在榻上。
“你是吾之胞妹，还是那呆子胞妹，还是那武夫的胞妹？”
李清韵不予理会，一脚将其踹开，舒服躺在榻上。
“也就只有你敢这样踹我！罢了罢了，谁让我只有你一个胞妹。”委屈的三皇子让出位置，静静护在公主身边。时序四月，天已生热，便持扇缓缓摇动，不敢有丁点声响。
此时恰有人送一便条，三皇子接过查看，竟是大皇子所送，上书：“今日皇妹好生威风。”三皇子有些怨气，怒道：“大皇子掖庭所出，又一跛脚，不详之人，你与他交际作甚？”
李清韵怒而起身，与三皇子对视：“你在背后，就如此对待兄长？”
“什么兄长？你明明知道，他为太子出谋，与太子为伍与我争斗！”
“那你为何要争斗？你们本是兄弟！”
“哪里是我们要斗？是陛……与你说了你也不懂！我不争，如何护得住你？”
李清韵起身将三皇子推出门外，怒将门关起。
”你不说，我也不想懂！我更无需你护！你舍了兄弟情谊也要去争那太子之位，那你去守着你的那堆谋士，给他们扇风去吧！“
一向说一不二的三皇子只得闷闷在门前跺脚，气无处撒，他怒而高喊：”都撤下去！我之精卫，在此处也是浪费！“
深宫皇后之处，正侍奉皇帝用膳的皇后，得闻公主府中护卫尽去，大喜。忙挑拨称太子将连同四皇子之边军造反，急需拿清韵公主入宫问话。迷得那年老昏聩的皇帝，忙交出了皇宫内卫的调动之权。
李清韵府中戒备已去，怎挡得住皇宫内卫？被抓入宫中，皇后下令，使其为己用，若不成，杀之。
却说三皇子撤去亲卫，很快便反悔。然就此一来一去之间，公主已被皇后捉入皇宫。无皇帝召见，凭三皇子一人，如何得入皇宫？再顾不得许多，三皇子分开差人，至大皇子、太子、四皇子处。
太子闻言，立至三皇子府中，将以太子权柄，二人速速共入宫中。
大皇子再无静气，多年所布朝中唇舌一夕尽用，传皇后谋逆，欲害君自立。
四皇子所囤城外之边军，全然不顾谋逆之罪，尽入城中，将皇宫团团围住。
三皇子多年所养死士，尽入皇城，于皇宫内卫欲加害公主之时将其救下。四位皇子协力，竟一朝改换新君，朝堂焕然。
后有书言：莫道皇天无情义，清韵一起止喧阗。皆道四子护社稷，不知皇女系心弦。
en:
"The grand army returns in triumph to pay respects to the Emperor! All carriages, clear the way!"
Banners blot out the sun above the streets of Chang'an. The Fourth Prince sits high upon a crimson charger, his armor gleaming, his spirit soaring. Truly the peerless young general of the Empire. He's come to the capital both to deliver news of the victory and to petition for rewards for the troops.
Just as the vanguard neared the capital, a rival set of imperial banners appeared on the horizon: it was the crown prince's carriage. The Fourth Prince's brow furrows. He had long heard that the Emperor harbored doubts toward the border legions. To send the Crown Prince to contest the road now, was this a ploy to suppress the army's rightful rewards? The border troops bled for this victory; their dead are beyond count. Should he yield to the Crown Prince and fail to secure honors befitting such a triumph, with what face could he return to the frontier? Resolute, he coolly ordered his aide, "Do not yield an inch. We enter the gates directly."
Under his canopy, the crown prince was equally troubled. His grasp on the throne was already tenuous. Today, led by some unknown design, he found his path blocked head-on by the Fourth Prince's triumphant return. To yield would not only erode his prestige among the princes but, more perilously, stoke the Emperor's suspicions against the military, a recipe for imperial disaster.
"Press on. We shall not be the first to retreat."
Amidst the bustling streets, a masked woman gazes toward the horizon. This is Li Qingyun, Princess of the Realm. Upon hearing that her Fourth Prince brother is returning to the capital, she knows she must be the first to welcome him home. As she waits by the roadside, an imperial guard hurries over with urgent news: "The Crown Prince and the Fourth Prince are set to collide at the gates. Neither will give way. Bloodshed may follow!"
Li Qingyun furrows his brow, pauses thoughtfully, and then commands, "Send my carriage now!"
The princess's carriage speeds down the main street, drawing closer to the border troops. Startled at first, the soldiers swiftly fall into formation. The Princess leaps onto the lead carriage. Seeing her silhouette, the vanguard general laughs heartily: "The Flying General is here! Clear the way!"
The Fourth Prince spurs his horse forward, his booming laughter echoing as he greets her. As it happened, the Princess had once donned male attire and slipped into the Fourth Prince's ranks. It was only amidst the heat of battle that he discovered his "soldier" was his own sister. Together they charged through blood and fire, forging a sibling bond tempered by the anvil of war. Utterly unbreakable. While she was a paragon of riding and archery, she possessed a catastrophic lack of direction. In the chaos of war, she would charge blindly through enemy lines, earning her the mocking, yet affectionate, title of "The Flying General."
Their joyful reunion speaks for itself. Learning the border troops' steadfast resolve, Li Qingyun contemplated the situation before resolutely drawing her brother back into the carriage.
"The border legions have their grievances, but our Second Brother's seat is equally precarious. If you trust me, Brother, board my carriage. Today, I shall escort both my brothers into the Imperial City together!"
"In this den of vipers we call a capital, if I cannot trust my own sister, I have no one left to believe in."
The carriage races forward, pulling up alongside the crown prince's procession. Yet, within the Crown Prince's personal retinue, a snake lay in wait. Seeing the Fourth Prince and the princess arrive together, he realized the plan was falling apart. Panicked, he drew his bow and fired an arrow straight at the Fourth Prince's face!
The Fourth Prince, a veteran of slaughters, did not even flinch. He snatched the arrow out of the air with a bare hand, a terrifying, murderous aura erupting from his silhouette.

As the traitor reached for a second shaft, the Crown Prince, pale with horror, roared for his execution. The man was cut down before he could draw the string again. The princess sensed the danger and glanced at the Fourth Prince, yet the Fourth Prince only tightened his arm around his sister, shielding her from the chaos. Not a single shadow of doubt crossed his face.
"Is this the extent of the struggle for the throne? Petty schemes and hidden arrows? Qingyun, if the capital stifles you, remember, the frontier is always open to you."
Knowing the gravity of the slight, the Crown Prince descended from his carriage and bowed deeply. "The failure to discipline my men is mine alone. Fourth Brother, I swear upon my life. This treachery was none of my doing!"
The Fourth Prince spared not a single look for the future Emperor. His gaze remained fixed solely upon the sister at his side. Only when the Princess offered a small, reassuring nod did the Fourth Prince relent. "I do not trust your word," he said coldly. "I trust only her."
The three of them entered the gates together within the Princess's carriage, a tableau of sibling unity that would be told and retold in the teahouses of Chang'an for years to come.
Little did they know that within the depths of the Inner Palace, the new Empress was trembling in a cold, thunderous rage. With the Fifth Prince still in his youth, the Empress knew her only path to power lay in the ruin of the four elder brothers. If they ceased their clashing, her ambitions would wither.
At the princess's residence, the Third Prince is waiting for her. The moment Li Qingyun walked in, the formidable Third Prince, a man who commands the court with an iron fist, shed his armor. He reveals his true self, sprawled across the daybed.
"Tell me, are you truly my sister by blood? Or do you belong to that dull-witted Crown Prince, or perhaps that oafish soldier of a Fourth Brother?"
Li Qingyun gave him a shove with her foot and flopped down comfortably.
"Only you would dare treat me so! But alas, such is my fate for having but one precious sister." Grumbling, the Third Prince scoots over. He hovers nearby like a scolded puppy, watching over her. The April air has begun to simmer with heat. He takes up a fan and wafts it with rhythmic gentleness, careful not to let even the slightest breeze disturb her peace.
Just then, a servant delivered a note. The Third Prince took it, glanced at the sender, and scowled. It was from the Eldest Prince. It read: "The princess impressed everyone today." The Third Prince's face soured instantly. "The Eldest Prince?" he spat. "He's just a cripple marked by misfortune! Why do you soil your hands by associating with such an ill-omened creature?"
Li Qingyun shot up, anger flashing in her eyes. "Is that how you talk about our own brother behind his back?"
"Our brother?" The Third Prince's voice turned sharp. "You know full well he's in the Crown Prince's pocket. He's against me!"
"Then why must this war continue? You share the same blood!"
"Do you think we chose this slaughter? It is the Empe...! You wouldn't understand. If I do not seize the crown, I cannot be the shield you need!"
Li Qingyun shoved him toward the door and then slammed it shut in his face.
"Then I don't want to understand! And I don't need your shield! If you're willing to throw away brotherhood just to claw your way to the top, then fine. Go ahead. Go back to your den of scheming advisors. Fan them with your lies and leave me in peace!"
The Third Prince, a man whose word is law in the capital, can only stomp his feet like a petulant child before her closed door. "Withdraw! Every last one of you! My elite guards are wasted on a house that does not want them!"
Back in the inner palace, news arrived that the Princess's residence now lay unguarded. A cold, predatory joy flickered in the Empress's eyes. Seizing the window of opportunity, the Empress dripped venomous lies into the Emperor's ear: she claimed the Crown Prince and the Fourth Prince were joining forces in a treasonous coup. Bewitched and senile, the Emperor fell for her web of deceit. In his dotage, he surrendered the authority to command the Palace Guard to her hands.
With her personal guards gone, the princess stood no chance against the palace troops. Once Qingyun was dragged within the palace walls, the Empress gave a cold mandate: break the Princess's will and bend her to the Empress's service, or end her life.
Meanwhile, the Third Prince had already begun to regret withdrawing his men. But by the time he realized his mistake, the princess had already been taken. Without an imperial summons, he couldn't set foot inside the palace alone. Casting caution to the wind, the Third Prince dispatched riders in every direction, to the Eldest, the Crown Prince, and the Fourth Prince.
The Crown Prince arrived at the Third's estate in a whirlwind. Armed with the Heir Apparent's seal and authority, the two brothers stormed the gates together.
The Eldest Prince cast aside his facade of serenity. He unleashed his vast network of court officials, the "tongues" he had cultivated for years, to brand the Empress a traitorous usurper.
The Fourth Prince abandoned all caution. Defying the laws of treason, he marched his battle-hardened border legions into the city, sealing the Imperial Palace in an iron ring of steel.
The Third Prince's private shadow-guard, warriors raised for this very hour, breached the inner sanctum. They struck just as the palace guards raised their blades against the Princess. United for the first time, the four princes staged a swift, bloodless coup. A new sovereign was crowned, and the rot of the old court was purged in a single morning.
"Seek not for warmth in the Heavens' cold decree, for Qingyun's cry stilled the sea of strife." "The world sings of four sons who saved the throne, unaware the Princess held the strings to their souls."

zh:
古乐没想到自己会和仇越海到这一步。
就像没想到当初会和他成为知音好友。
这段友谊以一种未曾想到的方式开启，又以一种未曾想到的方式结束，万般造化，不由人辩。

一切的起因，是那个女孩远行前，请求他不要告诉仇越海。
并不是有什么隔阂，只是不希望他因此涉险。
若是仇大哥知道了，定会不管不顾地吵着要一同去吧。她笑着说。
你就不一样，你素来克制。
是啊，素来克制。
素来克制的古乐，便替她保守秘密，便看着她远去，然后失去她的行踪。
那个女孩的下落成了一个谜题，一个无法对仇越海说出口的谜题。
为何说不出口？一是答应过那人，二是……他实在内疚。

他原打算等找到谜题的答案再告诉好友，所以在好友转身离去时一言不发，只身前往茫茫的江湖寻找答案。
后来，历经多年的艰辛，他终于找到了那个答案。
但当他将女孩的枯骨轻轻收拢怀中时，他发现，答案甚至比谜题本身更无法对好友开口。
有些谎，一说就是一辈子。
他只能看着仇越海愤恨地远去，只能长叹一声，将故事的辛酸都留给自己。
en:
Gu Le never imagined things would end this way with Qiu Yuehai.
Just as he never imagined they'd become bosom friends in the first place.
Their friendship had begun in an unexpected way and now ended in one too—such is the capriciousness of fate, beyond human reckoning.

It all started with the girl's request before she left: Don't tell Qiu Yuehai.
It wasn't that they had a quarrel. She just didn't want to drag him into danger."If Big Brother Yuehai knew, he'd charge headlong after me," she'd said with a laugh.
"But you—you've always been restrained."
Yes. Restrained. And so, restrained as ever, Gu Le kept her secret. Watched her leave. Then lost her trail entirely.
The girl's whereabouts became a mystery—one he couldn't bring himself to share with Qiu Yuehai.
Why? First, he'd promised. Second, the guilt was too heavy.

He'd intended to reveal the truth once he found answers himself. So when Qiu Yuehai turned away, Gu Le stayed silent and vanished into the jianghu alone.
Years later, after untold hardship, he finally uncovered the answer.
But when he gathered the girl's bones gently into his arms, he realized the truth was even harder to confess than the mystery itself.
Some lies become lifelong burdens.
All he could do was watch Qiu Yuehai leave in anger, heave a long sigh, and bury the story's bitterness in his own heart.

zh:
【子罕第九】

子罕言利与命与仁。
达巷党人曰：“大哉孔子！博学而无所成名。”子闻之，谓门弟子曰：“吾何执？执御乎？执射乎？吾执御矣。”
子曰：“麻冕，礼也。 今也纯， 俭，吾从众。拜下，礼也，今拜乎上，泰。 虽违众，吾从下。”
子绝四：毋意，毋必，毋固，毋我。
子畏于匡，曰：“文王既没，文不在兹乎？天之将丧斯文也，后死者不得与于斯文也。天之未丧斯文，匡人其如予何？”
太宰问于子贡曰：“夫子圣者与？何其多能也？”子贡曰：“固天纵之将圣，又多能也。”子闻之，曰：“太宰知我者乎？吾少也贱，故多能鄙事。君子多乎哉？不多也。”
牢曰：“子云：‘吾不试，故艺。’”
子曰：“吾有知乎哉？无知也。有鄙夫问于我，空空如也。 我叩其两端而竭焉。”
子曰：“凤鸟不至，河不出图，吾已矣夫。”
子见齐衰者、冕衣裳者与瞽者，见之，虽少者，必作，过之，必趋。
颜渊喟然叹曰：“仰之𣃥高，钻之𣃥坚，瞻之在前，忽焉在后。夫子循循然善诱人，博我以文，约我以礼。欲罢不能，既竭吾才，如有所立卓尔。虽欲从之，未由也已。”
子疾病，子路使门人为臣。病间，曰：“久矣哉，由之行诈也。无臣而为有臣，吾谁欺？欺天乎？且予与其死于臣之手也，无宁死于二三子之手乎？且予纵不得大葬，予死于道路乎？”
子贡曰：“有美玉于斯，韫椟而藏诸？求善贾而沽诸？子曰：“沽之哉！沽之哉！我待贾者。”
子欲居九夷，或曰：“陋，如之何？子曰：“君子居之，何陋之有？”
子曰：“吾自卫反于鲁，然后乐正，雅颂各得其所。”
子曰：“出则事公卿，入则事父兄，丧事不敢不勉，不为酒困，何有于我哉？”
子在川上曰：“逝者如斯夫，不舍昼夜。”
子曰：“吾未见好德如好色者也。”
子曰：“譬如为山，未成一篑，止，吾止也。譬如平地，虽覆一篑，进，吾往也。”
……
en:
【Book IX: Zi Han】

Zi Han seldom spoke of profit, fate, or benevolence.
A man from the village of Daxiang said, "Great indeed is Confucius! He is learned in many things, yet he has not made a name for himself in any one." When Confucius heard this, he said to his disciples, "What shall I take up? Shall I take up charioteering? Or shall I take up archery? I think I will take up charioteering."
The Master said, "A linen cap is prescribed by the rules of ceremony, but now a silk one is worn. It is economical, and I follow the common practice. To bow before ascending the steps is prescribed by the rules of ceremony, but now they bow after ascending. This is arrogant. Though it is contrary to the common practice, I bow before ascending."
There were four things from which the Master was entirely free. He had no foregone conclusions, no arbitrary predeterminations, no obstinacy, and no egoism.
When the Master was in danger from the people of Kuang, he said, "Since the death of King Wen, has not the cause of truth rested here with me? If Heaven had wished to let this cause of truth perish, then I, a future mortal, should not have got such a relation to that cause. While Heaven does not let the cause of truth perish, what can the people of Kuang do to me?"
The Grand Minister asked Zi Gong, saying, "Is your Master a sage? How is it that he is so skilled in many things?" Zi Gong said, "Certainly Heaven intended him to become a sage, and also made him skilled in many things." When the Master heard of this, he said, "Does the Grand Minister know me? When I was young, my condition was low, and therefore I acquired my ability in many things. But does a superior man need to have many skills? He does not need many."
Lao said, "The Master said, 'Having no official employment, I acquired many arts.'"
The Master said, "Am I indeed possessed of knowledge? I am not knowing. But if a mean person, who appears quite empty-like, asks anything of me, I set it forth from one end to the other, and exhaust it."
The Master said, "The Feng bird does not come; the river sends forth no map. It is all over with me!"
When the Master saw a person in mourning dress, or anyone in full ceremonial dress, or a blind person, on observing them, even if they were younger, he would rise up, and if he had to pass by them, he would do so hastily.
Yan Yuan, in admiration of the Master's doctrines, sighed and said, "I looked up to them, and they seemed to become more high; I tried to penetrate them, and they seemed to become more firm; I looked at them before me, and suddenly they seemed to be behind. The Master, by orderly method, skillfully leads men on. He enlarged my mind with learning, and taught me the restraints of propriety. When I wish to give over the study of his doctrines, I cannot do so, and having exerted all my ability, there seems something to stand right up before me; but though I wish to follow and lay hold of it, I really find no way to do so."
The Master being very sick, Zi Lu asked the disciples to act as ministers to him. During a remission of his illness, he said, "Long has the conduct of You been deceitful! By pretending to have ministers when I have them not, whom should I impose upon? Should I impose upon Heaven? Moreover, than that I should die in the hands of ministers, is it not better that I should die in the hands of you, my disciples? And though I may not get a great burial, shall I die upon the road?"
Zi Gong said, "There is a beautiful gem here. Should I lay it up in a case and keep it? Or should I seek for a good price and sell it?" The Master said, "Sell it! Sell it! But I would wait for one who knows the value."
The Master was wishing to go and live among the nine wild tribes of the east. Someone said, "They are rude. How can you do such a thing?" The Master said, "If a superior man dwelt among them, what rudeness would there be?"
The Master said, "I returned from Wei to Lu, and then the music was reformed, and the pieces in the Royal Songs and Praise Songs all found their proper places."
The Master said, "Abroad, to serve the high ministers and nobles; at home, to serve one's father and elder brothers; in all duties to the dead, not to dare not to exert one's self; and not to be overcome of wine—which one of these things do I attain to?"
The Master standing by a stream, said, "It passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night!"
The Master said, "I have not seen one who loves virtue as he loves beauty."
The Master said, "The prosecution of learning may be compared to what may happen in raising a mound. If there want but one basket of earth to complete the work, and I stop, the stopping is my own work. It may be compared to throwing down the earth on the level ground. Though but one basketful is thrown at a time, the advancing with it is my own going forward."

江湖传闻，那火爆勾栏戏院的《千里送京娘》，便是这《飞龙记》改出来的本子，赵大哥听了瞠目结舌，跑去问蒲先生是真是假，蒲先生也只是支支吾吾——

en:
Master Pu did indeed serve as a tutor for a time, and the reason, in short, was his repeated failure in the imperial exams.
Gossips often whispered that he had no real learning, but Big Zhao would argue for hours if he overheard such slander.
"Failing the exams doesn't mean lacking knowledge," he'd insist. "Master Pu knows everything under heaven and has unique insights. He's more like a Know-it-all!

Master Pu lived up to Big Zhao's faith. In recent years, he'd penned The Record of the Soaring Dragon through relentless writing at home. 
Rumor had it that the hit opera Chivalrous Escort in the Fair Grounds theaters was adapted from this very book. Big Zhao stared in disbelief and asked if it was true, but Master Pu only hedged.
"Never mind that! Have some roast pork first."

zh:
决断公事，要见起争之因，方能原情定罪也。据高庆诉，李二窃其玉镯一只。玉镯为高庆妻佩也，某日晨起，高氏视腕，镯不见矣。高氏云昨夜四更方寐，须臾辄醒，未曾摘取，亦不曾听得响动。高庆疑李二所为，率家丁往搜，果获人赃。
据李二供，本人为高庆佃户，租下等田地九亩。因水旱歉收，不得粮米，欠租未纳。李二仅有亡妻所遗陪嫁玉镯一只，高庆取之作抵。然镯非他窃，乃江湖人所为。其人听李二嗟叹道旁，知其失宝，故为他窃。其人未知姓名，诨号“金玉手”，当夜金玉手即还镯于李二，嘱咐好生收藏，免得事发，然仍被高庆寻得。
金玉手，余有所闻，衙门亦积有数案，未曾拿得此贼。余观李二常年务农，身态老拙，无上梁之能；高庆墙院内亦无窃贼痕迹。故高庆诉李二偷窃，难落实证。然李二既以镯抵债，又知金玉手将行窃，未加制止，且受赃物，念在初犯，不论盗窃，杖二十，玉镯归还高庆。金玉手取榜通缉，拿住本人后并案审之，再行处置。
en:
To adjudicate a dispute, one must trace its origins to weigh intent and assign blame. Gao Qing accuses Li Er of stealing a jade bracelet belonging to his wife. One morning, Madam Gao noticed the bracelet missing from her wrist. She testified that she had fallen asleep during the fourth watch and awoke shortly after, never removing the bracelet nor hearing any disturbance. Suspecting Li Er, Gao Qing led servants to search his home and allegedly recovered the stolen item.
Li Er's testimony reveals that he is Gao Qing's tenant, farming nine mu of poor-quality land. After crop failures from floods and droughts, he fell behind on rent. His sole possession was a jade bracelet, his late wife's dowry, which Gao Qing seized as collateral. However, Li Er claims the bracelet was not stolen by him but by a Swordsman who overheard his lamentations. This man, known only by the alias "Meridian Touch," stole the bracelet that very night but returned it to Li Er, urging him to hide it well. Yet Gao Qing found it anyway.
Of Meridian Touch, I have heard. The yamen has several unsolved cases involving him. Li Er, a lifelong farmer, is physically frail and lacks the agility for rooftop theft. Moreover, Gao Qing's compound shows no signs of forced entry. Thus, Gao Qing's accusation lacks solid evidence.  
However, Li Er accepted the bracelet as debt payment, knew of the impending theft, and failed to intervene. Though not guilty of theft, he harbored stolen goods. Considering his clean record, he is spared theft charges but sentenced to twenty strokes. The bracelet is returned to Gao Qing. A warrant is issued for Meridian Touch; upon capture, his cases will be consolidated for further judgment.

zh:
她已经见过太多人，太多次春色的轮替，太多颠沛流离的人，太多身怀秘密的人，这些人有的怀璧其罪，不等开口便消失于世间，有些人知晓一二真相便洋洋自得，横死于某夜某时。
世人总觉得自己在把玩秘密。
一个秘密往往比持有秘密的人活得更久。
知道秘密的人死了，而秘密却依旧活着，等待着下一个来使用它的人，再送走下一个使用它的人，性命如春亦逝，秘密却万古长存，但$N不一样。
$N有秘密，但却不像是一个会死在秘密里的人，似乎能走过许多春色轮替之时，走到比一个秘密更久的地方。
这样的人，比一个秘密更值得她的目光。
en:
She has seen too many faces, too many cycles of seasons, too many drifters adrift, too many souls hoarding secrets. Some bear treasures that seal their fate, vanishing before a word can be spoken. Others preen with half-truths, only to meet their end on some random night. 
Mortals always think they toy with secrets. 
A secret often outlives its bearer. 
When the knower dies, the secret persists—waiting for the next to wield it, then sending them off in turn. Lives fade like spring, but secrets endure. 
She harbors secrets, but doesn't seem the type to perish from them. She walks through more seasons than most, treading where secrets dare not last. 
A being like that... is worthier of her gaze than any secret.

en: A third of spring has slipped by unnoticed. Over the trellis, raspberry vines burst into cascades of blooms. A guest arrives to find no feast prepared, so I gather rain-drenched sprays instead. Lin Hong, author of Home-style Dishes in Mountainous Areas, once sampled raspberry flower congee during a visit with Lingjiu Temple's monks. The recipe reads: "Pluck the petals, blanch them in licorice root broth, then simmer with cooked congee." Favored by monastic communities, the congee balances bitterness with floral richness. Beyond roseleaf raspberries, Song Dynasty gourmands also infused plum blossoms, orchids, chrysanthemums, and osmanthus in congee.

zh:
【大学第四十二】

大学之道，在明明德，在亲民，在止于至善。知止而后有定，定而后能静，静而后能安，安而后能虑，虑而后能得。物有本末，事有终始。知所先后，则近道矣。
古之欲明明德于天下者，先治其国。欲治其国者，先齐其家。欲齐其家者，先修其身。欲修其身者，先正其心。欲正其心者，先诚其意。欲诚其意者，先致其知。致知在格物。物格而后知至，知至而后意诚，意诚而后心正，心正而后身修，身修而后家齐，家齐而后国治，国治而后天下平。自天子以至于庶人，壹是皆以修身为本。其本乱而末治者否矣。其所厚者薄，而其所薄者厚，未之有也。此谓知本，此谓知之至也。
所谓诚其意者，毋自欺也。如恶恶臭，如好好色，此之谓自慊。故君子必慎其独也。小人闲居为不善，无所不至，见君子而后厌然，掩其不善而著其善。 人之视己，如见其肺肝然，则何益矣。此谓诚于中，形于外，故君子必慎其独也。 曾子曰：“十目所视，十手所指，其严乎！”富润屋，德润身，心广体胖，故君子必诚其意。
《诗》云：“瞻彼淇澳，菉竹猗猗。有斐君子，如切如磋，如琢如磨。 瑟兮僴兮，赫兮喧兮。有斐君子，终不可谖兮。”“如切如磋”者，道学也。 “如琢如磨”者，自修也。“瑟兮僴兮”者，恂傈也。“赫兮喧兮”者，威仪也。“有斐君子，终不可谖兮”者，道盛德至善，民之不能忘也。《诗》云：“於乎，前王不忘！”君子贤其贤而亲其亲，小人乐其乐而利其利，此以没世不忘也。
《康诰》曰：“克明德。”《大甲》曰：“顾諟天之明命。”《帝典》曰： “克明峻德。”皆自明也。汤之《盘铭》曰：“苟日新，日日新，又日新。”《康诰》曰：“作新民。” 《诗》曰：“周虽旧邦，其命维新。”是故君子无所不用其极。《诗》云：“邦畿千里，维民所止。”《诗》云：“缗蛮黄鸟，止于丘隅。” 子曰：“于止，知其所止，可以人而不如鸟乎？”《诗》云：“穆穆文王，於缉熙敬止！”为人君，止于仁；为人臣止于敬；为人子，止于孝；为人父，止于慈； 与国人交，止于信。子曰：“听讼，吾犹人也。必也使无讼乎！”无情者不得尽其辞，大畏民志。此谓知本”。
所谓修身在正其心者，身有所忿懥，则不得其正，有所恐惧，则不得其正， 有所好乐，则不得其正，有所忧患，则不得其正。心不在焉，视而不见，听而不闻，食而不知其味。此谓修身在正其心。
所谓齐其家在修其身者，人之其所亲爱而辟焉，之其所贱恶而辟焉，之其所畏敬而辟焉，之其所哀矜而辟焉，之其所敖惰而辟焉。故好而知其恶，恶而知其美者，天下鲜矣。故谚有之曰：“人莫知其子之恶，莫知其苗之硕。”此谓身不修，不可以齐其家。
所谓治国必先齐其家者，其家不可教而能教人者，无之。故君子不出家而成教于国。孝者，所以事君也；弟者，所以事长也；慈者，所以使众也。《康诰》 曰：“如保赤子。”心诚求之，虽不中，不远矣。未有学养子而后嫁者也。一家仁，一国兴仁；一家让，一国兴让；一人贪戾，一国作乱，其机如此。此谓一言偾事， 一人定国。尧、舜率天下以仁，而民从之。桀、纣率天下以暴，而民从之。其所令反其所好，而民不从。是故君子有诸己而后求诸人，无诸己而后非诸人。所藏乎身不恕，而能喻诸人者，未之有也。故治国在齐其家。《诗》云：“桃之夭夭， 其叶蓁蓁。之子于归，宜其家人。”宜其家人，而后可以教国人。《诗》云：“ 宜兄宜弟。”宜兄宜弟，而后可以教国人。《诗》云：“其仪不忒，正是四国。” 其为父子兄弟足法，而后民法之也。此谓治国在齐其家。
所谓平天下在治其国者，上老老而民兴孝，上长长而民兴弟，上恤孤而民不倍，是以君子有絜矩之道也。所恶于上，毋以使下，所恶于下，毋以事上；所恶于前，毋以先后；所恶于后，毋以从前；所恶于右，毋以交于左；所恶于左，毋以交于右；此之谓絜矩之道。《诗》云：“乐只君子，民之父母。”民之所好好之，民之所恶恶之，此之谓民之父母。《诗》云：“节彼南山，维石岩岩。赫赫师尹，民具尔瞻。”有国者不可以不慎，辟，则为天下僇矣。《诗》云：“殷之未丧师，克配上帝。仪监于殷，峻命不易。”道得众则得国，失众则失国。
是故君子先慎乎德。有德此有人，有人此有土，有土此有财，有财此有用。德者本也，财者末也。外本内末，争民施夺。是故财聚则民散，财散则民聚。是故言悖而出者，亦悖而入；货悖而入者，亦悖而出。《康诰》曰：“惟命不于常。”道善则得之，不善则失之矣。《楚书》曰：“楚国无以为宝，惟善以为宝。”舅犯曰：“亡人无以为宝，仁亲以为宝。”
……
en:
[Book 42, The Great Learning]

What the Great Learning teaches, is to illustrate illustrious virtue; to renovate the people; and to rest in the highest excellence. The point where to rest being known, the object of pursuit is then determined; and, that being determined, a calm unperturbedness may be attained to. To that calmness there will succeed a tranquil repose. In that repose there may be careful deliberation, and that deliberation will be followed by the attainment of the desired end. Things have their root and their branches. Affairs have their end and their beginning. To know what is first and what is last will lead near to what is taught in the Great Learning.
The ancients who wished to illustrate illustrious virtue throughout the kingdom, first ordered well their own states. Wishing to order well their states, they first regulated their families. Wishing to regulate their families, they first cultivated their persons. Wishing to cultivate their persons, they first rectified their hearts. Wishing to rectify their hearts, they first sought to be sincere in their thoughts. Wishing to be sincere in their thoughts, they first extended to the utmost their knowledge. Such extension of knowledge lay in the investigation of things. Things being investigated, knowledge became complete. Their knowledge being complete, their thoughts were sincere. Their thoughts being sincere, their hearts were then rectified. Their hearts being rectified, their persons were cultivated. Their persons being cultivated, their families were regulated. Their families being regulated, their states were rightly governed. Their states being rightly governed, the whole kingdom was made tranquil and happy. From the Son of Heaven down to the mass of the people, all must consider the cultivation of the person the root of everything besides. It cannot be, when the root is neglected, that what should spring from it will be well ordered. It never has been the case that what was of great importance has been slightly cared for, and, at the same time, that what was of slight importance has been greatly cared for. This is called knowing the root. This is called the perfection of knowledge.
What is meant by "making the thoughts sincere" is the allowing no self-deception, as when we hate a bad smell, and as when we love what is beautiful. This is called self-enjoyment. Therefore, the superior person must be watchful over oneself when one is alone. There is no evil to which the mean person, dwelling retired, will not proceed, but when one sees a superior person, one instantly tries to disguise oneself, concealing one's evil, and displaying what is good. The other beholds one, as if one saw one's heart and reins—of what use is one's disguise? This is an instance of the saying—"What truly is within will be manifested without." Therefore, the superior person must be watchful over oneself when one is alone. The disciple Zeng said, "What ten eyes behold, what ten hands point to, is to be regarded with reverence!" Riches adorn a house, and virtue adorns the person. The mind is expanded, and the body is at ease. Therefore, the superior person must make one's thoughts sincere.
In the Book of Poetry, it is said, "Look at that winding course of the Qi, with the green bamboos so luxuriant! Here is our elegant and accomplished prince! As we cut and then file; as we chisel and then grind: so has he cultivated himself. How grave is he and dignified! How majestic and distinguished! Our elegant and accomplished prince never can be forgotten." That expression—"As we cut and then file"—the work of learning. "As we chisel and then grind"—indicates that of self-culture. "How grave is he and dignified!"—indicates the feeling of cautious reverence. "How commanding and distinguished!"—indicates an awe-inspiring deportment. "Our elegant and accomplished prince never can be forgotten"—indicates how, when virtue is complete and excellence extreme, the people cannot forget them. In the Book of Poetry, it is said, "Ah! the former kings are not forgotten." Future princes deem worthy what they deemed worthy, and love what they loved. The common people delight in what delighted them, and are benefited by their beneficial arrangements. It is on this account that the former kings, after they have quitted the world, are not forgotten.
In the Announcement to Kang, it is said, "He was able to make his virtue illustrious." In the Tai Jia, it is said, "He contemplated and studied the illustrious decrees of Heaven." In the Canon of the emperor (Yao), it is said, "He was able to make illustrious his lofty virtue." These passages all show how those sovereigns made themselves illustrious. On the bathing tub of Tang, the following words were engraved: "If you can one day renovate yourself, do so from day to day. Yea, let there be daily renovation." In the Announcement to Kang, it is said, "To stir up the new people." In the Book of Poetry, it is said, "Although Zhou was an ancient state, the ordinance which lighted on it was new." Therefore, the superior person in everything uses one's utmost endeavors. In the Book of Poetry, it is said, "The royal domain of a thousand li is where the people rest." In the Book of Poetry, it is said, "The twittering yellow bird rests on a corner of the mound." The Master said, "When it rests, it knows where to rest. Is it possible that a person should not be equal to this bird?" In the Book of Poetry, it is said, "Profound was King Wen. With how bright and unceasing a feeling of reverence did he regard his resting places!" As a sovereign, he rested in benevolence. As a minister, he rested in reverence. As a son, he rested in filial piety. As a father, he rested in kindness. In communication with his subjects, he rested in good faith. The Master said, "In hearing litigations, I am like any other body. What is necessary is to cause the people to have no litigations." So, those who are devoid of principle find it impossible to carry out their speeches, and a great awe would be struck into people's minds—this is called knowing the root.
What is meant by, "The cultivation of the person depends on rectifying the mind" may be thus illustrated: If one be under the influence of passion one will be incorrect in one's conduct. One will be the same, if one is under the influence of terror, or under the influence of fond regard, or under that of sorrow and distress. When the mind is not present, we look and do not see; we hear and do not understand; we eat and do not know the taste of what we eat. This is what is meant by saying that the cultivation of the person depends on the rectifying of the mind.
What is meant by "The regulation of one's family depends on the cultivation of one's person" is this: People are partial where they feel affection and love; partial where they despise and dislike; partial where they stand in awe and reverence; partial where they feel sorrow and compassion; partial where they are arrogant and rude. Thus it is that there are few people in the world who love and at the same time know the bad qualities of the object of their love, or who hate and yet know the excellences of the object of their hatred. Hence it is said, in the common adage, "A person does not know the wickedness of one's son; one does not know the richness of one's growing corn." This is what is meant by saying that if the person be not cultivated, one cannot regulate one's family.
What is meant by "In order rightly to govern the state, it is necessary first to regulate the family" is this: It is not possible for one to teach others, while one cannot teach one's own family. Therefore, the ruler, without going beyond one's family, completes the lessons for the state. There is filial piety—therewith the sovereign should be served. There is congenial submission—therewith elders and superiors should be served. There is kindness—therewith the multitude should be treated. In the Announcement to Kang, it is said, "Act as if you were watching over an infant." If a mother is really anxious about it, though she may not hit exactly the wants of her infant, she will not be far from doing so. There never has been a girl who learned to bring up a child, that she might afterwards marry. From the loving example of one family a whole state becomes loving, and from its courtesies the whole state becomes courteous, while, from the ambition and perverseness of the one person, the whole state may be led to rebellious disorder—such is the nature of the influence. This verifies the saying, "Affairs may be ruined by a single sentence; a kingdom may be settled by its one person." Yao and Shun led on the kingdom with benevolence and the people followed them. Jie and Zhou led on the kingdom with violence, and people followed them. The orders which these issued were contrary to the practices which they loved, and so the people did not follow them. On this account, the ruler must oneself be possessed of the good qualities, and then one may require them in the people. One must not have the bad qualities in oneself, and then one may require that they shall not be in the people. Never has there been a person, who, not having reference to one's own character and wishes in dealing with others, was able effectually to instruct them. Thus we see how the government of the state depends on the regulation of the family. In the Book of Poetry, it is said, "That peach tree, so delicate and elegant! How luxuriant is its foliage! This girl is going to her husband's house. She will rightly order her household." Let the household be rightly ordered, and then the people of the state may be taught. In the Book of Poetry, it is said, "They can discharge their duties to their elder brothers. They can discharge their duties to their younger brothers." Let the ruler discharge one's duties to one's elder and younger brothers, and then one may teach the people of the state. In the Book of Poetry, it is said, "In one's deportment there is nothing wrong; one rectifies all the people of the state." Yes; when the ruler, as a father, a son, and a brother, is a model, then the people imitate one. This is what is meant by saying, "The government of one's kingdom depends on one's regulation of the family."
What is meant by "The making the whole kingdom peaceful and happy depends on the government of one's state" is this: When the sovereign behaves to one's aged, as the aged should be behaved to, the people become filial; when the sovereign behaves to one's elders, as the elders should be behaved to, the people learn congenial submission; when the sovereign treats compassionately the young and helpless, the people do the same. Thus the ruler has a principle with which, as with a measuring square, one may regulate one's conduct. What a person dislikes in one's superiors, let one not display in the treatment of one's inferiors; what one dislikes in inferiors, let one not display in the service of one's superiors; what one hates in those who are before one, let one not therewith precede those who are behind one; what one hates in those who are behind one, let one not bestow on the left; what one hates to receive on the left, let one not bestow on the right—this is what is called "The principle with which, as with a measuring square, to regulate one's conduct." In the Book of Poetry, it is said, "How much to be rejoiced in are these princes, the parents of the people!" When a prince loves what the people love, and hates what the people hate, then is one what is called the parent of the people. In the Book of Poetry, it is said, "Lofty is that southern hill, with its rugged masses of rocks! Greatly distinguished are you, O grand-teacher Yin, the people all look up to you." Rulers of states may not neglect to be careful. If they deviate to a mean selfishness, they will be a disgrace in the kingdom.
In the Book of Poetry, it is said, "Before the sovereigns of the Yin dynasty had lost the hearts of the people, they could appear before God. Take warning from the house of Yin. The great decree is not easily preserved." This shows that, by gaining the people, the kingdom is gained, and, by losing the people, the kingdom is lost. On this account, the ruler will first take pains about one's own virtue. Possessing virtue will give one the people. Possessing the people will give one the territory. Possessing the territory will give one its wealth. Possessing the wealth, one will have resources for expenditure. Virtue is the root; wealth is the result. If one make the root one's secondary object, and the result one's primary, one will only wrangle with one's people, and teach them rapine. Hence, the accumulation of wealth is the way to scatter the people; and the letting it be scattered among them is the way to collect the people. And hence, the ruler's words going forth contrary to right, will come back to one in the same way, and wealth, gotten by improper ways, will take its departure by the same. In the Announcement to Kang, it is said, "The decree indeed may not always rest on us"; that is, goodness obtains the decree, and the want of goodness loses it. In the Book of Chu, it is said, "The kingdom of Chu does not consider that to be valuable. It values, instead, its good people." Duke Wen's uncle, Fan, said, "Our fugitive does not account that to be precious. What one considers precious is the affection due to one's parent."

zh: 泰山三美汤，乃鲁中泰安之传统名馔，其“三美”者，非指珍馐美器，实为三样至朴至简之物：泰山白菜、泰山豆腐与泰山泉水。此汤之成名，与泰山作为帝王封禅圣地之历史密不可分。据《旧唐书》所载，唐高宗封禅泰山时，其斋食便是以白菜、豆腐炖制而成。一道寻常素食，因登天子之席，便平添了几分神圣意蕴，泰山豆腐亦由此得“神豆腐”之美誉。
en: The Three-Delicacy Soup of Mount Tai is a renowned traditional dish from the Tai'an region. The "three delicacies" do not refer to exotic ingredients or exquisite tableware, but rather to three exceedingly pure and simple elements: Mount Tai cabbage, Mount Tai tofu, and Mount Tai spring water. The soup's fame is inextricably linked to Mount Tai's history as a sacred site for imperial sacrifices. According to the Old Book of Tang, when Emperor Gaozong performed the sacrifices at Mount Tai, his vegetarian court meals consisted of this very cabbage and tofu simmered into a clear, soothing broth. Because an ordinary vegetarian dish graced the Son of Heaven's table, it gained a touch of sacred charm, earning Mount Tai tofu the beautiful moniker of "Divine Tofu."

Fear causes essence to retreat, closing the upper burner; Qi rebounds downward, causing distention in the lower burner, thus Qi stagnates. Cold closes the pores, halting Qi flow, thus Qi contracts. Heat opens the pores and causes excessive sweating, thus Qi is lost. Fright isolates the heart and scatters the spirit; thoughts become unsettled, thus Qi becomes chaotic. Overthinking fixates the mind, anchoring the spirit and halting Qi's natural flow, thus Qi becomes knotted.

zh:
橘缘是一只母猫。
数月前，一只瘦削的橘猫忽然出现在佛光顶，还不知怎地爬上了佛光顶的塔尖。
清玄师父与一众僧侣十分担心，既担心猫儿不慎跌落伤及性命，又担心猫儿无意中碰到塔顶的秘物。
后来还是小摩诃想办法将猫儿引了下来，于是此猫在佛光顶扎根，池塘的鱼儿不知被它叼去多少。
猫儿要吃鱼，鱼儿要吃虫。众僧只得在水边日日念诵《往生咒》。
猫儿吃鱼无数，体态越发圆润。僧人们虽怨它杀生，却也怜它可爱，便为它取名“橘缘”。
橘缘，橘缘，橘猫与众生有缘，于少侠是佳缘，于池中的鱼儿便是孽缘了吧。
en:
Citrus Fate is a female tabby. 
A few months ago, she suddenly appeared at Halo Peak. And somehow managed to climb up to the tip of the tower. 
Master Qingxuan and the monks feared she might fall, or disturb the sacred relics at the peak. 
In the end, Little Mohe managed to lure her down. Since then, she has stayed at Halo Peak, helping herself to more than a few of the pond's fish. 
Cats eat fish, fish eat bugs, and so the monks began reciting the Rebirth Sutra by the water's edge. 
Despite their concerns about killing, they couldn't resist her charm, and named her "Citrus Fate".
For the tabby cat has fate with all beings: good karma with the young hero, bad karma for the pond fish.
Might as well have a drink...

zh:
……贞观十九年，玄奘法师自天竺携大小乘佛教经律论共五百二十夹，六百五十七部，宣讲教义，自此佛法盛行。开元四年，于清河善妙洲设法华禅院、永福禅院，藏经论共七十五部一千三百三十五卷。
先考篆之，祖考惠之第四子，开元六年率弟子周子晖、潘子冈、谢志松等十余人不远万里而来，落脚石工镇，比邻法华禅院，遥望永福禅院，专攻佛雕一道。初时所呈佛祖、观音、诸菩萨石像，徒有雕工而无神韵，先考云：“欲精佛雕，先悟佛理。”故诸人于禅院苦读佛法经纶，终有所得。此后所呈佛雕，颇具宝相庄严。石工镇由此名声大噪，更名慈心镇。杨、周、潘、谢四族自此方于慈心镇落地生根。
既有根基，必有根系，有根有底方为底蕴。族之有谱犹如国之有史也，后人观之，方知先祖不易，故立此族谱，以示传承。
……
惠之老祖子系
杨昌之、杨为之、杨敏之、杨纂之
……
惠之老祖孙系
杨纂之长子 杨惜艺
……
（此后十数页，均为杨氏一族谱系，自杨惠之起，传承至今已有十七代）
……
惠之老祖十六世孙 
杨道悯、杨道槐、杨道信……
惠之老祖十七世孙 
杨小郎、杨一来、杨小幺……
en:
In the 19th year of the Zhenguan era, the monk Xuanzang returned from India with 520 bundles of Mahayana and Theravada scriptures, comprising 657 texts, spreading Buddhist teachings far and wide. By the 4th year of the Kaiyuan era, the Fahua Temple and Yongfu Temple were established in Qinghe's Sundara Land, housing 75 scriptural collections totaling 1,335 volumes.
Zhuanzhi (fourth son of the patriarch Yang Hui) arrived in Metta Town in Kaiyuan 6th year with disciples including Zhou Zihui, Pan Zigang, and Xie Zhisong. Settling near the Fahua Temple and Yongfu Temple afar, they devoted themselves to Buddhist sculpture. Their early statues of Buddha, Guanyin, and bodhisattvas were technically adept but lifeless. Zhuanzhi declared: "To master Buddhist carving, one must first comprehend Buddhist truth." After intensive scripture study, their later works radiated divine majesty. Stonemason Town, renamed "Mercyheart Town", gained renown, and the Yang, Zhou, Pan, and Xie clans took root. Roots define heritage. A family without records is like a nation without history. This genealogy ensures descendants remember their ancestors' trials.

这儿却不一样。
这儿的天，比北边暖和些，用不着再裹厚厚的毛领。
这儿的地，比北边灿烂些，有事没事，就能肆意打滚。
这儿的狗，也有着许多从没见过的性子，有的爱喝酒，有的爱追猫，还有的养了许许多多小狗。
既然如此喜欢这里，那当然——
要带新认识的好朋狗回北方看雪了！

北边的雪很大很大，等把坏人全都赶跑，也还没化呢。
en:
Whitie's home is in the far, far north.
This time, Whitie is coming with Tiezi to fight the worst of the bad guys.
In past years at this time, snowflakes larger than dog fur would fall, covering the ground in white so deep not even a paw print remained.

But here, it's different.
The sky here is warmer than in the north; there's no need for thick fur collars.
The ground here is more vibrant than in the north; he can roll around freely whenever he likes.
The dogs here have many personalities he's never seen before: some love to drink, some love to chase cats, and some raise many, many puppies.
Since he loves it here so much, then of course...
He'll take his new best friends back north to see the snow!

The snow in the north is very, very deep, and it won't melt even after all the bad guys are driven away.

刚到青葱里，一踏上田埂，就被一对老农和书生拉着瞧他们搭伙种的葱！
耕读耕读，说来也奇，垄上的葱苗排得齐整，还真像学堂里练字的格子。
在集市上喝了两碗酒，晕乎乎的。青葱里的风，有葱香，有酒香，有墨香。连路边的石头，怕是也听过几句“关关雎鸠”吧？
在青葱里晃了几日，把葱王争霸的热闹看了，惠民义集的吆喝听了。想在耕读村多住些时候，听文津馆的人说话真有意思。要是能在这租半垄地，白天锄葱，晚上翻书，不走了也好，可惜江湖还有太多美景没看。
葱能下酒，书能醉人。总之这地方，来对啦！
en:
The moment I arrived at Greenshade Village and set foot on the field ridges, an old farmer and a young scholar grabbed me to show off the leeks they had grown together!
Ploughing and reading, ploughing and reading. Strange as it sounds, the leek shoots on the ridge were planted so neatly they looked exactly like the grids used for calligraphy practice in an academy.
After downing two bowls of wine at the market, my head was spinning delightfully. The wind blowing through Greenshade Village carries the scent of leeks, the aroma of wine, and the fragrance of ink. I suspect even the stones by the roadside have memorized the classic verses of the cooing ospreys.
I wandered around the village for a few days, watching the lively Crownleek Contest and listening to the hawkers at the Benevolence Bazaar. I found myself wanting to stay longer in this farming and studying village, simply because listening to the folks from the Inkbound Order talk is so endlessly fascinating. If only I could rent half an acre of land here: farming leeks by day, turning the pages of books by night. It would be fine to never leave. Alas, the martial world still holds too many beautiful sights unseen.
Leeks pair well with wine, and books intoxicate the soul. All in all, coming to this place was the right choice!

zh:
铁铁收：
铁铁，最近咋样啊？
从前搁咱家有钱花不出去，我老五脊六兽的了，大宅子，买了。大马车，有了。樊楼，去了……那些个好玩意儿，我老早就腻歪了，钱太多的痛你懂不，是真憋屈啊！
但这回来九流门，可就不一样了。这里的人个个都是人才，说话又好听，我贼喜欢这儿。
就说前天吧，一个人破衣娄嗖拄着拐杖，跟我说五个兄弟连同爹爹都战死了，嫂嫂们被抓去军营一去不回，留下八十老母和一堆侄儿侄女要养活，问我能不能帮帮忙。我听完眼泪八叉的啊，把盘缠抓一把大的都给了他。那家伙儿老高兴了，一把把拐杖扔了跑了，嘴里还吵吵：“大善人赏钱了，大善人赏钱了！”诶嘛，一颗火热的心，是真滴能唤起医学奇迹啊！
我数了数，来九流门这老些天，我拢共帮了二十八个九流门弟子，花了一百零八万通宝。铁铁，九流门的人是真滴过挺惨啊！
就是有一件事，让我心里不咋得劲。前几天门口老收到情书，有个叫范祺茶的九流门搁信里哥哥长，哥哥短，一直说什么：“哥哥，能跟鼠鼠谈恋爱吗？”看这人这么真诚我就答应了，临了见面才发现咋是个膀大腰圆的大汉啊！气得我赶紧跑了，骗我钱可以，但骗我感情不行！
铁铁，兄弟难受啊！啥也憋说了，你来九流门“掉到钱眼里”找我，我把剩下的通宝全给你。来陪兄弟唠会嗑吧，呜呜呜~
方旭留
en:
To my Bro:
Bro, how've you been?
Back home, I had money I couldn't even spend. I was bored out of my mind! Big mansion? Bought it. Grand carriage? Got it. Revelry Hall? Been there... I got sick of all those fancy things ages ago. Do you know the pain of having too much money? It's downright suffocating!
But coming to the Nine Mortal Ways is a whole different story. The people here are all so talented, and they speak so nicely. I freakin' love it here.
Take the day before yesterday. A guy in rags, leaning on a crutch, told me his five brothers and dad all died in battle, his sisters-in-law were taken to the army camp and never returned, leaving an eighty-year-old mother and a bunch of nieces and nephews to feed. He asked if I could help. Hearing that, my eyes welled up with tears, and I gave him a huge handful of coins. The guy was so happy he threw his crutch away and ran off, hollering: "The great benefactor gave me money!" Man, a warm heart truly can awaken medical miracles!
I counted. In the days I've been at the Nine Mortal Ways, I've helped 28 Nine Mortal Ways disciples, spending a total of 1.08 million coins. Bro, the folks at the Nine Mortal Ways really have it rough!
There's just one thing that rubs me the wrong way. A few days ago, I kept getting love letters at my door. Some Nine Mortal Ways disciple named Fan Qicha kept calling me "big bro" in the letters, saying things like, "Big bro, want to date this little kid?" Seeing how sincere they were, I agreed. But when we finally met, I found out it was a burly, broad-shouldered dude! I was so mad I ran away instantly. Swindle my coin if you must, but don't play with my heart!
Bro, I'm hurting! Say no more, come find me at the "Money Hole" in the Nine Mortal Ways. I'll give you all my remaining coins. Just come keep your bro company and chat for a bit, boohoo!
Yours, Fang Xu

zh:
奎奎曾经是禁军苟葛中最看好的一只小狗。
苟葛自诩阅犬无数，在禁军中相犬颇有一番威望。
兵书有云：“恐敌人夜间乘城而上，城中城外每三十步悬大灯于城半腹，置警犬于城上，吠之处需加备脂油火炬。”
机警的狗儿能闻出不对劲，提醒人们多加进警备，防止宵小进犯。
奎奎身高腿长，鼻子灵，性子机警，精力旺盛，不怕人——想来是在宫中成就一番事业的！
进宫一个月后，苟葛承认自己看错狗了。
某月三日，不好清洁，躁动难驯，洗澡时将禁军苟狄抓伤。
某月五日，奎奎训练时殴打同僚，造成它狗身体轻伤，情绪重伤，一蹶不振，不愿出勤。
巡查时萎靡低落，下班精神抖擞，日日如此，毫无长进。

汪汪汪，汪汪汪——（此处省略一千汪）
“大伙儿叫我奎奎。昨天又和帮我洗澡的人玩耍了，但他好像不怎么高兴的样子。
为了鼓励人，舔了他的脸，人用袖子快把脸搓秃噜皮了。”
“和大鲁比赛，大鲁弱，打输了不理狗，没意思。”
“宫里真好玩，被捡进宫里真好!”

苟葛对奎奎苦口婆心：“说你呢，注意当差态度！”
他看着自己寄予厚望的神犬，咧着嘴吐着舌头，摇头晃脑地打转。
也罢也罢。不是神犬又如何呢？奎奎开心就好。
en:
Kuikui was once the most promising pup in the Palace Guard kennels. Gou Ge prides himself on having judged countless dogs, and his eye for hounds carries real weight among the guards.

As one military text puts it: "Fearing the enemy may scale the walls at night, hang large lanterns every thirty paces along the wall's midline, and station watchdogs on the ramparts. Wherever they bark, reinforce the watch with oil-fed torches."
A sharp dog can scent trouble early and warn the guards to tighten patrols and keep prowlers out.

Kuikui is tall and long-legged, with a keen nose, quick instincts, boundless energy, and zero fear of people. Surely it was going to make something of itself in the palace.

One month later, Gou Ge admitted he had picked the wrong dog.

Day 3 (date redacted): hates being cleaned, restless and hard to handle. Scratched Guard Gou Di during a bath.
Day 5 (date redacted): started a fight during training. The other dog suffered minor physical injury and major emotional damage, then refused to report for duty.

On patrol, it's listless and low. Off duty, it's suddenly full of pep. Day after day, no improvement.

Woof woof woof, woof woof woof... (one thousand woofs omitted)

"Everyone calls me Kuikui. Yesterday I played with the person who bathed me again, but they didn't look very happy."
"So I licked their face to cheer them up, and they scrubbed their cheek raw with their sleeve."
"I raced Big Lu. Big Lu is weak. It lost and wouldn't play with me after. Boring."
"The palace is so fun. Getting picked up and brought here is the best!"

Gou Ge tried to reason with it: "I'm talking to you. Fix your attitude on duty!"
He watched the “miracle hound” he had pinned his hopes on, grinning with its tongue out, wobbling in place as it spun in circles.

Fine. Fine.
Miracle hound or not, as long as Kuikui is happy.

Moonlight still falls as it did years ago, but the chisel's song is gone. The crowds—whole or broken—have vanished. Only Jiu'er remains: a sleek shadow with eyes like polished jade.
 
No one knows why Jiu'er stays, or remembers it. Those who once cared are like shattered jade, quietly sinking into time's river. The workshop is empty and cold, yet Jiu'er remains. 
At least one cat still carries the memory of that broken jade shard beneath the waves—the shimmering pool reflecting the years they shared.

zh:
选手须遵守《燕云十六声》通用赛事规则，详见燕云十六声赛事中心官网【通用赛事规则】一栏。

比赛中游侠的部分战斗属性进行调平（角色和武学等级为90级，心法为6重，奇术为6重9段，解锁当前赛季所有通用型止戈天赋），战斗规则沿用天下争鸣玩法规则。

海选赛开放时间内报名参赛的战队需要自行前往争鸣赛海选界面参与匹配，完成10场海选比赛，成绩审核期24h，次日16:30审核结束，排名前32名的战队进入下一阶段比赛。
参赛战队将根据胜场进行排名，胜场较高的战队排名靠前，若胜场相同则比较胜场平均存活选手数量，胜场平均存活选手数量较多的战队排名在前，若胜场平均存活选手数量相同则比较胜场平均用时，胜场平均用时较短的选手排名靠前。

小组赛比赛开始前15分钟参赛战队可组队并由队长进入准备场景（需确保5人皆为战队成员），海选晋级战队分为4个小组进行单循环积分赛，采用三局两胜制。
【1】匹配机制：系统将于14:00开始自动为各战队匹配未对阵过的对手，奇数战队数量的小组首领会出现轮空寻找对手较长的情况。
【2】匹配流程：每次返回准备场景后，系统会持续进行新一轮匹配，由于仅匹配未交战的对手，可能出现等待时间较长的情况，请耐心等待。
【3】单循环赛制：需与小组内所有战队完成一轮对阵，小组赛将在所有战队完成相互对阵后结束。\审核时间结束后各小组第一名晋级八强胜者组、第二名晋级八强败者组，奖励在审核期结束后领取。
参赛战队将根据胜场进行排名，胜场较高的选手排名靠前；若胜场相同则比较净胜分（净胜分=所有小场胜场-所有小场负场），净胜分较高的选手排名靠前；若净胜分相同，则将对比双方的胜负关系。
若出现三名或以上选手胜场数与净胜分均相同，则仅计算这些战队之间的相互比赛结果，再按照上述规则依次比较，若仍无法区分，则比较小循环内胜利用时，用时较短的一方排名靠前。
en:
Players must abide by the Where Winds Meet General Tournament Rules. See the [General Tournament Rules] section on the official Where Winds Meet Tournament Center website. 

Combat attributes will be balanced during the match (Character and Martial Arts Level 90, Inner Ways Tier 6, Mystic Skill Tier 6 Stage 9, all current season general Arena Talents unlocked). Combat rules follow the 5v5 Arena rules. 

Teams registered during the Qualifiers period must proceed to the Contention Tournament Qualifiers interface to match. Complete 10 qualifying matches. Result review period is 24h, ending the next day at 16:30. The top 32 teams advance to the next stage. Teams are ranked by wins (higher is better). If wins are equal, compare average surviving players per win (more is better). If that is equal, compare average time per win (shorter is better).

Participating teams can form a team and enter the preparation scene via the leader 15 minutes before the Group Stage match starts (ensure all 5 members are in the team). Qualifying teams are divided into 4 groups for a Single Round Robin tournament, using a Best of 3 format. 
[1] Matchmaking: The system will automatically match teams against opponents they haven't fought yet starting at 14:00. Groups with an odd number of teams may experience longer wait times due to byes. 
[2] Process: After returning to the preparation scene, the system will continue to match for the next round. Wait times may be longer as it only matches opponents not yet fought. Please wait patiently. 
[3] Round Robin: Teams must complete a match against every other team in the group. The Group Stage ends when all teams have fought each other. After the review time ends, the 1st place of each group advances to the Top 8 Winners Bracket, and the 2nd place advances to the Top 8 Losers Bracket. Rewards are claimed after the review period. 

Team Ranking Criteria (Priority):
Participants are ranked by wins (higher is better). If wins are equal, compare Net Score (Net Score = Total Game Wins - Total Game Losses); higher Net Score ranks higher. If Net Score is equal, compare the Head-to-Head result.

If three or more players have equal wins and Net Scores, calculate results only among these players using the rules above. If still indistinguishable, compare time taken for wins in the small cycle; shorter time ranks higher.

zh:
十八岁那年，山夫带着两个弟弟寻到一座破庙。
庙里供的是谁，他们不知道。三张一模一样的脸朝着神仙，他们拜了三拜，齐声立誓：俺们要在江湖上闯出名头！
怎么闯？山夫说：“杀人。杀最恶的人。”
他们揭了张悬赏，画的是个刺客，据说杀过许多人。杀千万人为恶，他们想，除了这恶人定然可以名扬天下。
那一夜，月亮被云遮得严严实实。他们摸到破庙外头，听见里头有人说话。山夫扒着墙缝往里瞧，看见了那个悬赏令上的人。
那人正站着，面前跪了一个。他声音平平的，像说一件无关紧要的事：“你替契丹人做事，杀我中原人，该杀。”
刀光一闪，干脆利落，像是切菜。那人收刀，侧目看来，目光正落在山夫怀里的悬赏令上。
“来领赏的？”
山夫扑通跪下了。他才知道他们错得彻底，杀人的未必是恶人，自己却险些做了恶人。
他把来龙去脉说了，那人沉默许久，长长一叹：“去青州吧，文津馆在那儿。学门手艺，也好谋生。”
三兄弟冲那人磕了三个响头，比拜神时虔诚得多。
山夫没读过书，只分得清最简单的善恶：杀契丹狗的，便是好人。好人说的话，大抵不会错。
他们乘船过河，到了泰山脚下。
须发皆白的老人正站在山道旁，呼喝一声，双臂发力，便将一名登山客直送到半山腰去。
三兄弟看呆了。山夫想，这就是他们要学的手艺。
“挑一下不？”老人问。
“俺们想拜你为师。”
“要挑就过来，不挑一边去。”
老人不再理他们，继续送人上山。
山夫跟了他三日三夜，絮絮叨叨地讲从小到大的事，讲三兄弟入江湖，讲那一夜破庙里险些杀错了人。
第三夜，老人终于回过头来。
“想跟，就跟吧。”
山夫跪下，就要磕头。老人伸手扶住了。
他说：“江湖太乱，国仇家恨，恩恩怨怨，一不小心就成了贼。我是不忍你等成贼。”
他顿了顿，又说：“挑山的本事却是真的。挑多少人，便是多少人。”
en:
When Shan Fu was eighteen, he and his two younger brothers stumbled upon a ruined temple.
They didn't know which god was worshipped there, but the three identical brothers looked up at the crumbling statue, bowed three times, and swore an oath in perfect unison: "We're going to be legends in the jianghu."
How exactly? Shan Fu had a plan: "We hunt down the worst people alive and kill them."
They tore down a bounty token for an infamous assassin with a massive body count. Killing a mass murderer, they figured, was justice. Taking down a villain like that would make them heroes overnight.
That night, thick clouds swallowed the moon. The brothers crept up to an abandoned shrine and heard voices inside. Peering through a crack in the wall, Shan Fu spotted the face on the token.
The assassin stood over a kneeling figure. When he spoke, his voice was flat, as if discussing the weather. "You sold out our people to the Khitans. You deserve to die."
A single flash of steel, clean and effortless. The assassin sheathed his sword and glanced sideways, his eyes locking dead onto the crumpled bounty token in Shan Fu's hands.
"Here to collect?"
Shan Fu hit the dirt, dropping to his knees. In a flash, he realized how wildly wrong they had been. A killer wasn't always a monster, and by trying to play the hero, Shan Fu had almost murdered a patriot.
Shaking, he confessed everything. The swordsman fell silent for a long time before letting out a heavy sigh. "Go to Qingzhou," he said. "Find the Inkbound Order. Learn a real trade and make an honest living."
The brothers knocked their foreheads against the floorboards, a far more genuine prayer than they'd offered the god earlier.
Shan Fu couldn't read, but his moral compass was simple: anyone who killed traitors was a good person. And a good person's advice was worth taking.
They took a boat across the river to the foot of Mount Tai.
Beside the steep mountain trail stood a white-haired, white-bearded old man. With a sharp grunt and a flex of his massive arms, he hoisted a traveler onto his carrying pole and hauled them up the steps with impossible ease.
The brothers stood there, slack-jawed. That, Shan Fu decided, was the trade they were going to learn.
"Need a lift?" the old man grunted.
"We want you to take us on as apprentices."
"If you're paying for a ride, get in. If not, get out of the way." The old man ignored them and went back to work.
Shan Fu dogged his steps for three days and three nights. He talked the old man's ear off about their childhood, their grand dreams of the jianghu, and how they had nearly murdered a righteous man in a ruined temple.
On the third night, the old man finally stopped and looked back.
"If you're going to follow me, then follow."
Shan Fu dropped to his knees to bow, but the old man caught him by the shoulders.
"The jianghu is a mess of blood feuds and politics," the old man said softly. "Take one wrong step, and you're just another bandit. I'd hate to see boys like you turn into thieves."
He paused, looking up the dark mountain. "But carrying people up these steps... that's real. The sweat is honest, and the weight you carry is true."

zh:
【僖公第五】

元年，春，王正月。
继弒君不言即位，正也。
○齐师、宋师、曹师次于聂北，救邢。
救不言次，言次，非救也。非救而曰救何也？遂齐侯之意也。是齐侯与？齐侯也。何用见其是齐侯也？曹无师，曹师者，曹伯也。其不言曹伯何也？以其不言齐侯，不可言曹伯也。其不言齐侯何也？以其不足乎扬，不言齐侯也。
○夏，六月，邢迁于夷仪。
迁者，犹得其国家以往者也。其地，邢复见也。
○齐师、宋师、曹师城邢。
是向之师也。使之如改事然，美齐侯之功也。
○秋，七月，戊辰，夫人姜氏薨于夷，齐人以归。
夫人薨不地。地，故也。不言以丧归，非以丧归也，加丧焉。讳以夫人归也，其以归，薨之也。
○楚人伐郑。
○八月，公会齐侯、宋公、郑伯、曹伯、邾人于柽。
○九月，公败邾师于偃。
不日，疑战也。疑战而曰败，胜内也。
○冬，十月，壬午，公子友帅师败莒师于丽，获莒挐。
莒无大夫，其曰莒挐何也？以吾获之目之也。内不言获，此其言获何也？恶公子之绐。绐者奈何？公子友谓莒挐曰:"吾二人不相说，士卒何罪？"屏左右而相搏。公子友处下，左右曰"孟劳。"孟劳者，鲁之宝刀也。公子友以杀之。然则何以恶乎绐也？曰弃师之道也。
○十有二月，丁巳，夫人氏之丧至自齐。
其不言姜，以其杀二子，贬之也。或曰"为齐桓讳杀同姓也"。

二年，春，王正月，城楚丘。
楚丘者何？卫邑也。国而曰城，此邑也，其曰城何也？封卫也。则其不言城卫何也？卫未迁也。其不言卫之迁焉何也？不与齐侯专封也。其言城之者，专辞也。故非天子不得专封诸侯，诸侯不得专封诸侯。虽通其仁，以义而不与也。故曰，仁不胜道。
○夏，五月，辛巳，葬我小君哀姜。
○虞师、晋师灭夏阳。
非国而曰灭，重夏阳也。虞无师，其曰师何也？以其先晋，不可以不言师也。其先者何也？为主乎灭夏阳也。夏阳者，虞虢之塞邑也。灭夏阳而虞虢举矣。虞之为主乎灭夏阳何也？晋献公欲伐虢，荀息曰:"君何不以屈产之乘、垂棘之璧而借道乎虞乎？"公曰:"此晋国之宝也。如受吾币而不借吾道，则如之何？"荀息曰:"此小国之所以事大国也。彼不借吾道，必不敢受吾币。如受吾币而借吾道，则是我取之中府而藏之外府，取之中厩而置之外厩也。"公曰:"宫之奇存焉，必不使受之也。"荀息曰:"宫之奇之为人也，达心而懦，又少长于君。达心则其言略，懦则不能强谏，少长于君，则君轻之。且夫玩好在耳目之前，而患在一国之后，此中知以上乃能虑之。臣料虞君，中知以下也。"公遂借道而伐虢。宫之奇谏曰:"晋国之使者，其辞卑而币重，必不便于虞。"虞公弗听，遂受其币而借之道。宫之奇谏曰:"语曰'唇亡则齿寒'，其斯之谓与！"挈其妻子以奔曹。献公亡虢，五年而后举虞。荀息牵马操璧而前曰:"璧则犹是也，而马齿加长矣！"
○秋，九月，齐侯、宋公、江人、黄人盟于贯。
贯之盟，不期而至者江人、黄人也。江人、黄人者，远国之辞也。中国称齐、宋，远国称江、黄，以为诸侯皆来至也。
○冬，十月，不雨。
不雨者，勤雨也。
○楚人侵郑。

……
en:
[Chapter 5: Lord Xi]

The first year, spring, the royal first month.
When succeeding a murdered ruler, not mentioning 'ascending the throne' is correct.
The armies of Qi, Song, and Cao halted at Niebei to rescue Xing.
An action of rescue does not normally mention a "halt". If it mentions a "halt," it means it was not a genuine rescue. If it was not a rescue, why does the text use the word "rescue"? It is to comply with and satisfy the intent of the Marquis of Qi. Was this entirely the Marquis of Qi's doing? Yes, it was the Marquis of Qi. How do we see that it was the Marquis of Qi? Cao actually had no army there; what is referred to as "the army of Cao" was merely the Earl of Cao himself. Why does the text not explicitly say "the Earl of Cao"? Because since the text did not explicitly mention the leader, the "Marquis of Qi," it could not inappropriately mention his follower, the "Earl of Cao." Why did it not explicitly mention the "Marquis of Qi"? Because his actions were not worthy of praise, the text does not mention the title "Marquis of Qi."
In summer, the sixth month, Xing relocated to Yiyi.
"Relocated" implies that they were still able to take their state institutions, altars, and people along with them. By explicitly naming the location, it signifies that the state of Xing re-manifested and survived in this new territory.
The armies of Qi, Song, and Cao built walls for Xing.
This was the very army that had previously attacked Xiang. Deploying them again felt like an entirely new enterprise, which praises the great achievement of the Marquis of Qi.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the wuchen day, the Lord's wife, Lady Jiang, passed away in Yi, and the people of Qi took her remains back.
When the Lord's wife passes away, the Annals normally does not explicitly name the location of her death. Naming the location indicates that her death was due to an abnormal cause. Because they did not actually return her as a deceased lady in a proper funeral manner; the text merely applied the term "funeral/remains" to her retrospectively out of courtesy. The text is concealing the shameful fact that she was extradited and brought back. By stating that the people of Qi "took her back," the text treats her death as the ultimate outcome that legally defined the return.
The people of Chu attacked Zheng.
In the eighth month, the Lord met with the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Earl of Zheng, the Earl of Cao, and a person of Zhu at Cheng.
In the ninth month, the Lord defeated the army of Zhu at Yan.
Not recording the day suggests uncertainty about the battle. Despite the uncertainty, calling it a defeat indicates that the home state was victorious.
In winter, the tenth month, on the renwu day, Prince You led the army and defeated the army of Ju at Li, capturing Ju Na.
The state of Ju normally does not have recognized grand masters, so why is this person explicitly named as "Ju Na"? It is because our state captured him, so he is identified specifically to emphasize the capture. The Annals normally does not use the word "captured" for internal operations, so why is it used here? It is to condemn the deception practiced by the Prince. What was this deception? Prince You said to Ju Na: "The two of us are displeased with one another, but what crime have our soldiers committed?" They dismissed their attendants and engaged in hand-to-hand combat. Prince You was pinned underneath, whereupon his hidden attendants called out, "Meng Lao!" Meng Lao being a legendary prized dagger of Lu. Prince You used it to kill Ju Na. If so, why does the Annals condemn this deception? Because it is a total abandonment of the righteous way of commanding an army.
In the twelfth month, on the dingsi day, the remains of the Lord's wife arrived from Qi.
Omitting her clan name Jiang serves to condemn her for the murder of the two princes. Others say it was to conceal the taboo of Lord Huan killing his own kinsmen.

In the second year, spring, the royal first month, the wall of Chu Qiu was built.
What was Chuqiu? It was a city of the state of Wei. Usually, the term "built walls" is used for a capital state, but this was merely a city; why does the text say "built walls"? Because it was the enfeoffment and reconstitution of the state of Wei. Then why does the text not simply say "built walls for Wei"? Because the state of Wei had not yet officially relocated there. Why does it not mention Wei's relocation? It is to avoid granting the Marquis of Qi the right to arbitrarily enfeoff or re-establish a state. Writing "built walls" is an expression of arbitrary, unilateral action. Therefore, none but the Son of Heaven may arbitrarily enfeoff lords, and feudal lords have no right to arbitrarily enfeoff other lords. Although the Annals acknowledges the benevolence of his action, out of supreme justice, it does not grant him the formal right. Hence it is said: "Benevolence cannot be allowed to override the Way."
In summer, the fifth month, on the xinsi day, our Lord's wife, Lady Aijiang, was buried.
The armies of Yu and Jin destroyed Xiayang.
Xiayang was not a capital state, yet the text uses the word "destroyed." Why? It is to emphasize the critical weight and strategic importance of Xiayang. Yu did not actually possess a full, standard army. Why does the text refer to it as an "army"? Because the state of Yu is listed before Jin in the phrasing, it was syntactically impossible not to use the word "army." Why is Yu placed before Jin? To condemn Yu as the primary instigator and collaborator in the destruction of Xiayang. Xiayang was a heavily fortified border town situated between Yu and Guo; with the fall of Xiayang, both Yu and Guo would inevitably be seized. Why did Yu act as the primary collaborator in destroying Xiayang? Duke Xian of Jin desired to launch a military campaign against Guo. His minister, Xun Xi, advised him: "Why does my Lord not offer the famed team of horses from Quchan and the precious jade disk of Chuiji to request a right of passage through the state of Yu?" The Duke replied: "These are the supreme treasures of the State of Jin. What if the Duke of Yu accepts our gifts but refuses to grant us the right of passage?" Xun Xi answered: "This is exactly how a small state serves a great state. If he intends to deny us passage, he will certainly not dare to accept our gifts. If he does accept our gifts and grants us passage, it is merely equivalent to taking our treasures from our inner treasury to store them in our outer treasury, or taking our horses from our inner stable to place them in our outer stable." The Duke objected: "Gong Zhiqi is present at the Yu court; he will surely never allow the Duke of Yu to accept them." Xun Xi responded: "As for the character of Gong Zhiqi, he is intellectually clear but faint-hearted, and moreover, he grew up alongside the Duke of Yu. Because his mind is clear, his speeches are concise and easily ignored; because he is faint-hearted, he is incapable of severe remonstrance; and because he grew up with the Duke, the Duke treats him lightly. Furthermore, when delightful playthings are right before one's eyes and ears, while a catastrophic threat lies far behind the security of the whole nation, none but those of above-average intelligence can foresee it. I assess the Duke of Yu to be of below-average intelligence." The Duke of Jin subsequently requested the path and attacked Guo. Gong Zhiqi remonstrated, saying: "The words of the Jin envoy are humble, yet their gifts are excessively heavy; this will surely bring no benefit to Yu." The Duke of Yu refused to listen; he accepted the gifts and granted them the right of passage. Gong Zhiqi remonstrated again, saying: "An old proverb says, 'If the lips are gone, the teeth will be cold.' Is this not exactly what it means!" He then packed up and took his wife and children to flee to the state of Cao. Duke Xian of Jin successfully destroyed Guo, and five years later, he swallowed up Yu as well. Xun Xi then led the horses and held the jade disk as he stepped forward to the Duke of Jin, saying: "The jade disk remains exactly as it was, but the horses' teeth have grown a bit older!"
In autumn, the ninth month, the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, a person of Jiang, and a person of Huang made a covenant at Guan.
Regarding the covenant at Guan, those who arrived voluntarily without prior appointment were the people of Jiang and the people of Huang. The phrasing "the people of Jiang and the people of Huang" is an expression reserved for distant states. The Central States are referred to as "Qi" and "Song," while the distant states are referred to as "Jiang" and "Huang"; this is to demonstrate that the feudal lords from all over the world, even from afar, came to attend.
In winter, the tenth month, it did not rain.
Writing "it did not rain" is an expression of deep anxiety and earnest longing for rain.
The people of Chu invaded Zheng.

未央城栽培了许多会寻宝的猫，可全天下会赏宝的猫，却唯有觅骨珍的“小泉泉”和“赏宝宝”而已。
小泉泉是一只严格的小猫，它最为出名的，就是那斜觑人的眼神。
来觅骨珍卖货的客商，最怕的就是它那眼神，露了那眼神，便是在怀疑了。一旦它开始怀疑，东西就多半要卖不出去。
在小泉泉这里，开门就是开门，不开门就是不开门，纵使客商给它再多小鱼干，也不会改变它的判断。
这也是任山重格外信任小泉泉的原因，只要听了它的叫声，就知道宝贝贵重与否。
一声喵叫开门，两声喵叫很开门，三声喵叫，那便是开到了南天门。
“猫在门口辛苦赏宝，猫好，人在棺材里睡大觉，人坏。”小泉泉想。
en:
Weiyang City is home to many treasure-hunting cats, but when it comes to appreciating fine treasures, none rival the famed pair—Quanquan and Shang Baobao. 
Quanquan and Shang Baobao from Bone Seeker.

Quanquan is a strict little cat,
best known for its signature sideways glare.

Merchants coming to Bone Seeker to sell their wares fear that look above all else. That look means suspicion. And once Quanquan starts doubting—your goods are as good as unsold.

With Quanquan, if an item is valuable, it's valuable; if it's a fake, it's a fake. No matter the amount of dried fish the merchants have to offer, it will not sway Quanquan's judgment.

That's exactly why Ren Shanzhong trusts the little cat so much. He only needs to hear its meow to know how valuable an item truly is. One meow means it's valuable, two meows means it's very valuable, three meows, well, it's valuable beyond one's imagination.

"The cat toils at the door identifying treasures. The cat is good. The human naps in a coffin. The human is bad." So thinks Quanquan.

“想飞？好咧！师父拉着你转悠悠！”年幼的张一豪笑得咧开嘴，被师父拉着抡甩好多圈。
“师父，还要！”张一豪笑着拍手，意犹未尽。
很多年后，师父早已霜鬓渐染，握刀的手也有些不稳。
张一豪也有了自己的小徒弟。
“师父，俺想飞！”小徒弟拉着张一豪的手，赖赖唧唧央告着。
“别赖叽。来，师父拉着你，转悠悠！”
小徒弟被抡甩起来的时候，他分明看到师父坐在台阶上，笑眯眯地看着自己。

Years later, with silvered hair and an unsteady hand, Zhang Yihao carried on the tradition with his own apprentice. In that joyful whirl, he seemed to glimpse his old master smiling, blessing the moment across years.

After the fall of the Later Liang to Li Cunxu, the personal guard of Zhu Wen was stripped of their weapons. This spear fell into the armory of Li Congrong. 
But during the chaos at Tianjin Bridge, Li Congrong was killed by An Congyi. The spear once again vanished into exile. 
Shi Shouxin recovered it on the battlefield. He had hoped to wield it in glorious campaigns. But peace had already settled across the realm. The cry of the wild geese, once sharp enough to pierce the skies, was now nothing but a fading echo. 
Before it could carve a new tale with its new master,
the spear was sealed away, a silent witness to the warrior's unspoken bitterness and regret.

zh:
【某月廿二日】
墨门研学，忌虚谈废务，浮文妨要。
此番入世游历，按照门规，归来之日以本心创作机关一件，游学方有始终。
入世三月有余，蓝图一片空白，毫无头绪，愧对师长。
为平心中愁绪，亦为照拂百姓，近日投身汴梁东郊，重拾儿时务农之乐。

【某月廿四日】
榫卯机巧可解，而拖延之心不可解。
田野之间，烦恼全消。种地。

【某月廿六日】
不潜心研究机关为苍生谋福，单凭一人一犁，何以耕天下？
丘影啊丘影，何等堕落！

【次月一日】
幸得农家小儿赠东田瓜一枚。
田壤排水受滞，甜味不佳。若以机巧之力引渠分流，或有改善。
种地。

【次月三日】
偶遇同门故人闫舒。此人心高气傲，墨守亭中多次与我相辩，知错不改，活该唤作闫王。
问及归门机关，似已成竹在胸。
可气，可恼。不如种地。

【次月五日】
再逢闫王。
“丘兄既得务农之乐，何不以灌溉为题？”
信口胡言，不安好心。此话……
颇有几分道理？

【次月十日】
墨者之学，贵在务实。木料一根，可支梁柱；残革半片，可缝衣履。
引渠犁地，却少刃锋。闫王送百炼钢。磁州精铁而制，好钢，好钢。
此人往日嘲讽无状，难得良心发现。

【秋月十日】
不负师长教诲，引渠机巧初成，尚需与同门商议改进。
即日归山。
欠下人情一桩，也该向姓闫的道谢。竟是多日不见。

【冬月十二日】
再未见过闫舒。
手札交予入世同门，附信一封，若见此人，烦代为转交。
en:
[22nd Day of the Month]
Mohist studies abhor empty talk; superficial words only delay real progress.
For this worldly journey, sect rules dictate I must return with a mechanism created from my true calling to complete my training.
I have been in the world for over three months. My blueprints are completely blank. I have no ideas, and I bring shame to my masters.
To ease my troubled mind and help the locals, I have recently headed to the eastern suburbs of Bianliang to rediscover the joy of farming I knew as a child.

[24th Day of the Month]
Mechanical puzzles can be solved, but a procrastinating heart cannot.
In the fields, all my worries disappear.
I shall farm.

[26th Day of the Month]
If I don't focus on inventing mechanisms for the greater good, how can I plow the world with just one man and one plow?
Qiu Ying, Qiu Ying, what a slacker you've become!

[1st Day of the Next Month]
A farm boy kindly gave me a melon from the east field.
The soil here drains poorly, making the fruit bland. If I use mechanisms to divert water into irrigation channels, it might help.
I shall farm.

[3rd Day of the Next Month]
Bumped into Yan Shu, an old peer from the sect. The man is arrogant and stubborn. We debated endlessly back at the pavilion, and he never admits defeat. He truly earns his nickname, "Yama Yan," tyrant of the underworld.
When I asked about his final project, he looked entirely too confident.
Irritating. Infuriating.
I'm going back to farming.

[5th Day of the Next Month]
Ran into Yama Yan again.
"Since you enjoy farming so much, Brother Qiu, why not make irrigation your project?"
He was just spouting nonsense to mock me. And yet...
He has a point?

[10th Day of the Next Month]
Mohist learning values the practical. A single log can become a pillar; a scrap of leather can mend a boot.
For my irrigation plow, I lacked a proper blade. Yan sent me a piece of hundred-forged steel. Pure Cizhou iron. Excellent steel.
Given his usual endless sarcasm, a sudden bout of conscience is rare.

[10th Day of Autumn]
I have honored my masters' teachings. The prototype of the irrigation mechanism is done, though it needs peer review.
I head back to the mountain today.
I owe Yan a debt of gratitude and should thank him, but surprisingly, he has been nowhere to be found for days.

[12th Day of Winter]
I still haven't seen Yan Shu.
I'm passing this journal to a disciple heading down the mountain, along with a letter. If you run into him, please deliver it.

zh:
我等时间，等了一辈子。 
等到手中的唐旗已暌违这片土地，近一个甲子。 
人言常道，五十而知天命。可我等的，并不是那个天命的安排。 
所以我与时间相争，哪怕背弃我的善良，滥用我的权术，牺牲……我的长兄。 
不，哪怕牺牲的是我。凉州可以无我，归义军可以无我， 
但那个誓心归国的愿望，还需要一个继任者。 
而今日，我便要等那个继任者到来。 
只是，我等的那个人，还存着赤子的热忱，和对我的敬重。 
长安的质子，不应是归义军领袖的软肋。 
故而，我告诉他真相，也告诉他龌龊。 
我希望他舍弃我，一如我舍弃兄长。 
如果权力的更迭都需要鲜血，那么就用我的血肉来为他造势。 
直到他凌驾我的旧部，取代我的威望。 
看着外面被他控制的亲兵，看着他压制那些不愿我归唐的声音。 
果然，他做得很好。 
我本以为，他来的时候，会把刀架在我的脖颈， 
可他却把刀递给了我—— 
我太熟悉这把刀，起初的那场送别，就是兄长将刀送予我， 
后来我又把它送还给兄长的儿子。 
而现在，这把刀又还至跟前。 
他说，他会带着归义军，等我回家。 
那一刻，我们洞谙彼此，我知道，此时、未来， 
不管千里、万里，我们还会站在彼此身旁。
en:
I have waited my entire life.
Waited until the Tang banner had been absent from this land for nearly sixty years.
People say a man knows his destiny by fifty. But what I awaited was not a destiny given by heaven.
So I fought against time itself, even if it meant betraying my kindness, abusing my power, and sacrificing... my own brother.
No, even if it meant sacrificing myself. Liangzhou can survive without me. The Guiyi Army can survive without me.
But the vow to return to our homeland demands a successor.
And today, I awaited that successor's arrival.

The man I wait for, however, still holds the passion of an idealist, and his respect for me.
A hostage in Chang'an cannot be the weakness of the Guiyi Army's leader.
So I showed him the truth, in all its glory and its filth.
I wanted him to forsake me, just as I forsook my brother.
If the transfer of power demands blood, then let my own flesh pave his way to greatness—
until he commands my old guard and his prestige surpasses my own.
I see his loyal soldiers outside. I see him silencing those who oppose our return to the Tang.
As expected, he has performed masterfully.

I thought he would come with a blade to my throat.
Instead, he offered the blade to me.
I know this blade. In our first parting, my brother gave it to me.
Later, I gave it to his son.
And now, it has returned to my hands.
He said he would lead the Guiyi Army, and wait for me to come home.
In that moment, we understood everything without a word. I know that now, and in the future, across a thousand miles or ten thousand, we will always stand by each other's side.

夜深了，龟奶奶颤抖着手拿出自己的聚宝盆，将里面的钱一个个排开。

最旧的两个开元通宝，还是大唐的钱。那时她才尚未及笄的年纪，战乱连年，日子难过，家里自然想着发卖了女儿，她不怨爹娘，她永远记得娘亲从那卖她的钱里捡出两枚塞进她手里时，滚烫的泪水落在她手背的感觉。买她的人家拽着她的手走了很远，她还能听到娘的哭声。她暗暗发誓，以后自己若是做了娘亲，绝不和自己的孩子分开。

旁边的天成元宝……曾是她的房子。那是后唐的事儿，官府忽然通告提高征缴屋税，她与相公交不起，只得将那体面的房子卖了，换了一手天成元宝，搬到了角门里去。

至于那些天福元宝……她将老大好好地送上了战场，可最后回来的却只有那一袋子大小不一的天福元宝。相公要拿那钱去换个新房子，她不许，她要留给她的盈盈，她绝不允许盈盈像她一样被卖到人家家去，她要盈盈明媒正娶地嫁出去，这些钱就做嫁妆，到时给盈盈盘个铺子，让她好歹不用再过清贫的日子。可没过多久，契丹人就来了，契丹人要钱，她不给，那是老大的命换来的，契丹人要砍掉她的头，她都闭了眼睛，可她那窝囊了一辈子的相公，却似大梦方醒了一般，和契丹人拼杀起来，保住了她和盈盈的命。大火烧尽之后，她和盈盈回到残损的房子，什么都没有了，只有那尸身早已冰冷发黑的老头子，手里还紧紧攥着一枚血淋淋的天福元宝。

其他的……就是那些唐钱了。这两年，市面上赚宋钱难，她起早贪黑，却也只赚了些唐钱。最难的时候，赚的速度，还比不上那唐钱跌价的速度，可她不灰心，只要自己还没死，她总要盈盈过上好日子，可是盈盈……她想到那周太祖进城的时候，四处喊着“屠城了”，“抢钱了”……盈盈拼了命要守住那天福元宝，她跑出去了，然后……然后……盈盈那红润的脸便变得白惨惨的，眼睛没了一点光泽，满身都是伤口……不不不，盈盈就在她身边呢，老大打仗要回来了，盈盈念了老大的信，老大要她们好好照顾自己，来日团聚呢……

想到这里，龟奶奶用粗糙的手背抹了一把眼睛，又将那聚宝盆里的钱一颗颗放了回去，听着那丁铃当啷的声音，她又感到有些盼头了。
en:
Late at night, Granny Turtle trembled as she took out her treasure basin, lining up the coins inside.

The two oldest Kaiyuan Tongbao coins were from the Tang Dynasty. She'd been a girl then, during endless wars. Her family had wanted to sell her, and she didn't blame them. She could still feel her mother's scalding tears falling on her hands as she pressed those two coins into them before the buyer dragged her away. She'd vowed that if she ever became a mother, she'd never be separated from her children.

Next to them lay Tiancheng Yuanbao... once her home. During the Later Tang, when the government suddenly raised housing taxes, she and her husband had sold their decent home for these coins, moving to the Forsaken Quarter.

The Tian Fu Yuanbao coins... she'd sent her eldest son to war with pride, only for a bag of mismatched coins to return in his place. Her husband had wanted to use them to buy a new house, but she'd refused. They were for Yingying, her daughter. She'd vowed Yingying would marry properly, not be sold like she had been. These coins would be her dowry, enough to open a shop and spare her poverty. But then the Khitans came. They'd demanded the coins, blood money from her son's death, and she'd rather die than give them up. Her meek husband had suddenly fought like a demon to protect her and Yingying. After the fire, they'd returned to ruins, finding only his cold, bloodied body still clutching a Tian Fu Yuanbao.

The rest were Tang Coins. These past two years, earning Song Coins had been hard. She'd risen before dawn and worked till dusk, only to watch the Tang Coins lose value faster than she could earn them. But she'd never lost hope, until Yingying... She remembered when Zhou Taizu's army entered the city, shouting "Massacre!" and "Loot!" Yingying had tried to protect the Tian Fu Yuanbao, running out... and come back pale, lifeless, covered in wounds... No, Yingying was here now, safe. Her eldest son would return from war soon. She'd read his letter telling them to stay alive for their reunion.

Wiping her eyes with a calloused hand, Granny Turtle dropped the coins back into the treasure basin, listening to their clatter. For a moment, hope flickered again.

【杂记下第二十一】

有父之丧，如未没丧而母死，其除父之丧也，服其除服。卒事，反丧服。虽诸父昆弟之丧，如当父母之丧，其除诸父昆弟之丧也，皆服其除丧之服。卒事，反丧服。如三年之丧，则既顈，其练祥皆同。王父死，未练祥而孙又死，犹是附于王父也。有殡，闻外丧，哭之他室。入奠，卒奠，出，改服即位，如始即位之礼。大夫、士将与祭于公，既视濯，而父母死，则犹是与祭也，次于异宫。既祭，释服出公门外，哭而归。其它如奔丧之礼。如未视濯，则使人告。告者反，而后哭。如诸父昆弟姑姊妹之丧，则既宿，则与祭。卒事，出公门，释服而后归。其它如奔丧之礼。如同宫，则次于异宫。
曾子问曰：“卿大夫将为尸于公，受宿矣，而有齐衰内丧，则如之何？”孔子曰：“出舍乎公宫以待事，礼也。”孔子曰：“尸弁冕而出，卿、大夫、士皆下之。尸必式，必有前驱。”
父母之丧，将祭，而昆弟死；既殡而祭。如同宫，则虽臣妾，葬而后祭。祭，主人之升降散等，执事者亦散等。虽虞附亦然。自诸侯达诸士，小祥之祭，主人之酢也哜之；众宾兄弟，则皆啐之。大祥：主人啐之，众宾兄弟皆饮之，可也。凡侍祭丧者，告宾祭荐而不食。
子贡问丧，子曰：“敬为上，哀次之，瘠为下。颜色称其情；戚容称其服。”请问兄弟之丧，子曰：“兄弟之丧，则存乎书策矣。”君子不夺人之丧，亦不可夺丧也。孔子曰：“少连、大连善居丧，三日不怠，三月不解，期悲哀，三年忧。东夷之子也。”
