菩提苦海，燥热异常，清河一线野外劳作者——铁心将军，此刻却依然坚守岗位。高温之下，为何他能身披铠甲，不畏酷暑？让我们走近菩提苦海，探寻铁心将军的消暑之秘！
“铁心将军，铁心将军？”
或许是我们的声音太轻，抑或是今日太热，将军不语，似在沉思。
“铁心将军！叶将军！”
将军依然不语，只是一味纹丝不动，风中似有一丝焦味传来……
正在众人束手无策之际，一神秘男子大步而来，手捧巨碗。将军接过，一饮而尽——霎时身形一振，寒光乍现，挥剑生风，气贯长虹！
据神秘男子介绍，碗中之物名曰“冰食”，能令好人活，热人也活！它究竟是何来历，为何有如此奇效？且听下回分解！
en:
Bodhi Sea, scorching and unbearable, yet General Ironheart toils relentlessly under the blazing sun along the Qinghe frontier. How does he endure the sweltering heat clad in armor? Let us venture into the Bodhi Sea and uncover the secret behind General Ironheart's summer survival!
"General Ironheart? General Ironheart?"
Perhaps our voices were too faint, or the day too stifling—the General remains silent, lost in thought.
"General Ironheart! General Ye!"
Still, he does not respond, standing motionless as a faint charred scent drifts on the wind...
Just as all seemed hopeless, a Mysterious Man strides forth, bearing an enormous bowl. The General takes it and downs its contents in one gulp—instantly revitalized, his blade gleams coldly as he swings it with a force that splits the air!
According to the Mysterious Man, the bowl held "Frostbite," a concoction that "revives the good and cools the scorched!" What is its origin, and how does it wield such power? And the Story Goes On...

我大受震撼，决定学习他走抽象派，不再追求形似，想追求一波神似。结果您猜怎么着！我那些雕刻的大作无人问津。真是让我百思不得其解。果然，搞抽象也是需要天赋的呀！
en:
Young Master, I've been out and about lately, picking up a few things, and it's really shown me how big the world is. A few days ago at Shicha Sea, I saw an old man selling wooden carvings. I looked closely and thought it was a tiger, but he said no. Then I guessed monkey. Still no. I kept guessing and only in the end found out it was a fox! And the strangest part? A whole crowd of people was rushing to buy those unrecognizable little carvings of his! Unbelievable!
It really shook me, so I decided to learn from him and go abstract with my creation. No more chasing a perfect likeness. I was going for spirit instead of form. And would you believe it? My great masterpieces didn't sell at all. I still can't figure it out. Looks like abstract art takes real talent, too!

zh:
入海口者，渤海之滨，河海襟喉也。其景甚伟，诗文不足以抒怀，唯直称“入海口”耳。黄河自昆仑发脉，贯九域而东注，挟泥沙以奔涌，终汇于此。其地襟带沧海，吞吐洪波，烟涛渺渺，若天堑无涯。昔为洪荒之野，芦荡莽苍，碱蓬匝地，赤霞铺野。每至天寒，蓬草尽染，绯红漫卷，与沧浪相映，蔚为奇观。

地当鹜集鹭翔之枢，实乃羽族天堂。众鸟越冬之径，咸汇于此。鹬鹬衔泥，雁阵蔽日，鹄鸣九皋，鸥戏清涟。泽畔蒹葭苍苍，汀间荻花瑟瑟，百禽或唳或栖，各得其所。洲渚星罗，溆港纵横，鱼跃藻荇，龟潜蒲丛，俨然混沌初开之象。

余观河海交汇处，黄涛浊浪与碧波相激，泾渭分明，若阴阳剖判，亘古不移。万物纷纭，终归自然。唯此碱滩红蓼，岁岁枯荣；群羽唳空，年年往复。天地之心，或在斯乎？
en:
The Seaward Gate rests upon the shores of the Bohai Sea, serving as the very throat and collar where river meets ocean. Its majesty is so profound that poetry and prose fall short of expressing its grandeur; thus, it is plainly named the Seaward Gate. Originating from Mount Kunlun, the Yellow River pierces through the Nine Provinces, flowing ever eastward. Surging with churning silt, it finally pours into this terminus. Here, the land embraces the vast sea, swallowing and exhaling torrential swells. The misty waves stretch into the boundless void, like an endless celestial chasm. In ancient times, this was a primal wilderness of sprawling reeds, where alkali flora blanketed the earth, paving the fields in a rosy glow. Whenever winter descends, the seepweeds are dyed a deep crimson, rolling and unfurling to mirror the azure waves. A spectacle of supreme wonder.

Situated as a vital hub for gathering egrets and soaring herons, this land is truly a paradise for the feathered tribes. The migratory paths of wintering birds all converge here. Snipes carry mud in their beaks, formations of wild geese obscure the sun, swans cry from the deep marshes, and gulls play in the clear ripples. Beside the waters, the green reeds stand lush and dense; on the shoals, the silver grass rustles in the wind. Hundreds of avian species call out or roost, each finding its rightful place. Islets are scattered like stars, creeks and channels crisscross the land, fish leap among the algae, and turtles hide within the rushes. It presents a scene akin to the very dawn of creation.

I observe the confluence of river and sea, where the muddy yellow torrents clash with the emerald waves. They remain distinct, like the severing of Yin and Yang, unchanging since antiquity. The myriad things, in all their chaotic glory, ultimately return to nature. Only the crimson seepweeds of these alkali flats wither and bloom with the years; only the flocks of birds cry to the sky, returning cycle after cycle.

Perhaps the very heart of Heaven and Earth resides right here.
Deluded Mortals

对于南门大街一小户人家来说，过日子，不如叫做讨生活，十几岁的张安康顶不喜欢这样的日子。
一家一户，一日三餐，几两碎银子算着用，手头有宽裕的时候，去铺子上买些折价的碎肉，便算是一餐好菜。
邻里多少有拌嘴的，今儿我家说了你家闲话，明儿东头和西头吵架，今儿晌午的一场雨，你家收了晾晒的铺盖，却没喊上我家一句，那下次遇上阴沉沉的天，遇上飞低了的虫鸟，我也不同你家说了。

张安康年岁小的时候，觉得这就是顶大的事儿，他年岁再大些的时候，便觉得这些人心眼小，这些破事怎么值得来回拉扯上几年，可他的日子里，只有这些小事，这地方太闷太小，他期待着顶大的事。
在他的印象里，顶大的事发生前，就和话本子里侠客出场一样，有惊天的动静。
可顶大的事在来之前，是安静的，没有潮湿的雨气，没有低飞的虫鸟，没有近乎凝固的空气。

一场屠城战火来临前的预兆，甚至小于开封城的一场雨。

来苏蒙学的钟声还在酉时三刻照常响起，街道的店铺依旧吵吵嚷嚷。
那时候很多人从未想过——世上大多人，想要拼死所求的到底是什么？
在几个时辰之后，这个问题却已不必想了。
对于有些人而言，他们拼死想要求来的事物，是曾经习以为常的某个平凡瞬间。
是一家一户，是一日三餐，是碎银几两，他们恳求日子重新寡淡到，一场雨的口角，便足以能拉扯几年。

别害怕，一场雨过后，开封城的大火将会熄灭。
不、这场火怎么会熄灭呢，用人命点燃的大火在记得他们的人死去前，是无法熄灭的。
它只是一小簇一小簇地分开，钻进了人的命运之中，然后长久地燃烧在无数人身躯之下，灼烧着无数人的一日，又一日。
en:
For a modest household on South Gate Avenue, life was less about living and more about scraping by, a kind of existence that teenage Zhang Ankang despised 
.A family, three meals a day, counting every scrap of silver. If they were lucky, they might buy discounted scraps of meat from the butcher, and that would be considered a feast.
The neighbors bickered endlessly. Today, one family gossiped about another. Tomorrow, the east end quarreled with the west. If it rained at noon and one household took in their laundry without warning the other, then next time the sky darkened or birds flew low, they'd return the silence.

When Zhang Ankang was young, he thought these were the most important matters in the world. As he grew older, he realized how petty people could be. Why waste years squabbling over such nonsense? But his life was made of these trifles. The place was stifling, too small. He longed for something big.
In his mind, before something big happened, there ought to be earth-shattering omens, like in the tales of wandering heroes.
But when the truly big things come, they arrive in silence. No damp prelude of rain, no low-flying insects, no suffocating tension in the air.

The omen of a massacre was quieter than a drizzle in Kaifeng City.

The bell of Hopewell Academy still rang at the usual hour. The streets buzzed with the clamor of merchants.
Back then, few had ever stopped to wonder: What is it that most people in this world would fight to the death for?
Within hours, that question would no longer need answering.
For some, the thing they'd give their lives to reclaim was once just an ordinary moment, taken for granted.
A home. Three meals a day. A handful of coins. They would beg for the return of a life so mundane that a quarrel over forgotten laundry could stretch on for years.

Don't be afraid. After the rain, the fires of Kaifeng City will burn out.
No, how could they? A fire kindled by human lives cannot be extinguished until the last who remember them are gone.
Instead, it fractures into tiny embers, seeping into the fabric of fate. It burns beneath the skin of countless souls, scorching their days, one after another.
Righteousness is important

zh:
【隐公下第一】

【经】
三年，春，王二月，己巳，日有食之。
○三月，庚戌，天王崩。
○夏，四月，辛卯，君氏卒。
○秋，武氏子来求赙。
○八月，庚辰，宋公和卒。
○冬，十有二月，齐侯、郑伯盟于石门。
○癸未，葬宋穆公。
【传】
三年，春，王三月，壬戌，平王崩。赴以庚戌，故书之。
○夏，君氏卒。声子也。不赴于诸侯，不反哭于寝，不祔于姑，故不曰薨。不称夫人，故不言葬。不书姓，为公故，曰君氏。
○郑武公、庄公为平王卿士。王贰于虢，郑伯怨王。王曰：“无之。”故周、郑交质。王子狐为质于郑，郑公子忽为质于周。王崩，周人将畀虢公政。四月，郑祭足帅师取温之麦。秋，又取成周之禾。周、郑交恶。
君子曰：“信不由中，质无益也。明恕而行，要之以礼，虽无有质，谁能间之？”苟有明信，涧溪沼沚之毛，苹蘩蕰藻之菜，筐筥锜釜之器，潢污行潦之水，可荐于鬼神，可羞于王公，而况君子结二国之信，行之以礼，又焉用质？风有采蘩、采苹，雅有行苇、泂酌，昭忠信也。”
○武氏子来求赙，王未葬也。
○宋穆公疾，召大司马孔父而属殇公焉，曰：“先君舍与夷而立寡人，寡人弗敢忘。若以大夫之灵，得保首领以没，先君若问与夷，其将何辞以对？请子奉之，以主社稷。寡人虽死，亦无悔焉。”对曰：“群臣愿奉冯也。”公曰：“不可。先君以寡人为贤，使主社稷，若弃德不让，是废先君之举也，岂曰能贤？光昭先君之令德，可不务乎？吾子其无废先君之功。”使公子冯出居于郑。八月庚辰，宋穆公卒，殇公即位。
君子曰：“宋宣公可谓知人矣。立穆公，其子飨之，命以义夫。商颂曰：‘殷受命咸宜，百禄是荷。’其是之谓乎！”
○冬，齐、郑盟于石门，寻卢之盟也。庚戌，郑伯之车偾于济。
○卫庄公娶于齐东宫得臣之妹，曰庄姜，美而无子，卫人所为赋硕人也。又娶于陈，曰厉妫，生孝伯，早死。其娣戴妫，生桓公，庄姜以为己子。公子州吁，嬖人之子也。○有宠而好兵，公弗禁，庄姜恶之。石碏谏白：“臣闻爱子，教之以义方，弗纳于邪。骄奢淫泆，所自邪也。四方之来，宠禄过也。将立州吁，乃定之矣，若犹未也，阶之为祸。夫宠而不骄，骄而能降，降而不憾，憾而能眕者，鲜矣。且夫贱妨贵，少陵长，远间亲，新间旧，小加大，淫破义，所谓六逆也。君义，臣行，父慈，子孝，兄爱，弟敬，所谓六顺也。去顺效逆，所以速祸也。君人者，将祸是务去，而速之，无乃不可乎？”弗听。其子厚与州吁游，禁之，不可。桓公立，乃老。

【经】
四年，春，王二月，莒人伐杞，取牟娄。
○戊申，卫州吁弑其君完。
○夏，公及宋公遇于清。
○宋公、陈侯、蔡人、卫人伐郑。
○秋，翚帅师会宋公、陈侯、蔡人、卫人伐郑。
○九月，卫人杀州吁于濮。
○冬，十有二月，卫人立晋。
【传】
四年，春，卫州吁弑桓公而立。
○公与宋公为会，将寻宿之盟。未及期，卫人来告乱。
○夏，公及宋公遇于清。
○宋殇公之即位也，公子冯出奔郑，郑人欲纳之。及卫州吁立，将修先君之怨于郑，而求宠于诸侯，以和其民，使告于宋曰：“君若伐郑以除君害，君为主，敝邑以赋与陈、蔡从，则卫国之愿也。”宋人许之。于是陈、蔡方睦于卫，故宋公、陈侯、蔡人、卫人伐郑，围其东门，五日而还。
公问于众仲曰：“卫州吁其成乎？”对曰：“臣闻以德和民，不闻以乱。以乱，犹治丝而棼之也。夫州吁，阻兵而安忍。阻兵无众，安忍无亲。众叛亲离，难以济矣。夫兵犹火也，弗戢，将自焚也。夫州吁弑其君而虐用其民，于是乎不务令德，而欲以乱成，必不免矣。”
○秋，诸侯复伐郑。宋公使来乞师，公辞之。羽父请以师会之，公弗许，固请而行。故书曰“翚帅师”，疾之也。诸侯之师败郑徒兵，取其禾而还。
○州吁未能和其民，厚问定君于石子。石子曰：“王觐为可。”曰：“何以得觐？”曰：“陈桓公方有宠于王，陈、卫方睦，若朝陈使请，必可得也。”厚从州吁如陈。石碏使告于陈曰：“卫国𥚹小，老夫耄矣，无能为也。此二人者，实弑寡君，敢即图之。”陈人执之，而请莅于卫。九月，卫人使右宰丑莅杀州吁于濮，石碏使其宰獳羊肩莅杀石厚于陈。
君子曰：“石碏，纯臣也，恶州吁而厚与焉。‘大义灭亲’，其是之谓乎！”
卫人逆公子晋于邢。冬，十二月，宣公即位。书曰“卫人立晋”，众也。

【经】
五年，春，公矢鱼于棠。
○夏，四月，葬卫桓公。
○秋，卫师入郕。
○九月，考仲子之宫，初献六羽。
○邾人、郑人伐宋。
○螟。
○冬，十有二月，辛巳，公子𫸩卒。
○宋人伐郑，围长葛。
【传】
五年，春，公将如棠观鱼者。臧僖伯谏曰：“凡物不足以讲大事，其材不足以备器用，则君不举焉。君，将纳民于轨物者也。故讲事以度轨量，谓之轨；取材以章物采，谓之物。不轨不物，谓之乱政。乱政亟行，所以败也。故春搜、夏苗、秋猕、冬狩，皆于农隙以讲事也。三年而治兵，入而振旅，归而饮至，以数军实。昭文章，明贵贱，辨等列，顺少长，习威仪也。鸟兽之肉，不登于俎，皮革、齿牙、骨角、毛羽，不登于器，则公不射，古之制也。若夫山林川泽之实，器用之资，皂隶之事，官司之守，非君所及也。”公曰：“吾将略地焉。”遂往，陈鱼而观之。僖伯称疾不从。书曰“公矢鱼于棠”，非礼也，且言远地也。
○曲沃庄伯以郑人、邢人伐翼，王使尹氏、武氏助之。翼侯奔随。
○夏，葬卫桓公。卫乱，是以缓。
○四月，郑人侵卫牧，以报东门之役。卫人以燕师伐郑。郑祭足、原繁、泄驾以三军军其前，使曼伯与子元潜军军其后。燕人畏郑三军，而不虞制人。六月，郑二公子以制人败燕师于北制。
君子曰：“不备不虞，不可以师。”
○曲沃叛王。秋，王命虢公伐曲沃，而立哀侯于翼。
○卫之乱也，郕人侵卫，故卫师入郕。
○九月，考仲子之宫，将万焉。公问羽数于众仲。对曰：“天子用八，诸侯用六，大夫四，士二。夫舞，所以节八音而行八风，故自八以下。”公从之。于是初献六羽，始用六佾也。
○宋人取邾田。邾人告于郑曰：“请君释憾于宋，敝邑为道。”郑人以王师会之，伐宋，入其郛，以报东门之役。宋人使来告命。公闻其入郛也，将救之，问于使者曰：“师何及？”对曰：“未及国。”公怒，乃止。辞使者曰：“君命寡人同恤社稷之难，今问诸使者，曰‘师未及国’，非寡人之所敢知也。”
○冬，十二月，辛巳，臧僖伯卒。公曰：“叔父有憾于寡人，寡人弗敢忘。”葬之加一等。
○宋人伐郑，围长葛，以报入郛之役也。

【Duke Yin, Part 1, Year 3-5】

【Classic】
Year 3, Spring, in the King's second month, on the day Jisi, there was an eclipse of the sun.
○In the third month, on the day Gengxu, the King of Heaven passed away.
○Summer, in the fourth month, on the day Xinmao, Lady Jun passed away.
○Autumn, a son of the Wu family came to request contributions for the funeral.
○In the eighth month, on the day Gengchen, Duke He of Song passed away.
○Winter, in the twelfth month, the Marquis of Qi and the Earl of Zheng made a covenant at Shimen.
○On the day Guiwei, Duke Mu of Song was buried.
【Commentary】
Year 3, Spring, in the King's third month, on the day Renxu, King Ping passed away. The announcement was made on the day Gengxu, so it was recorded accordingly.
○Summer, Lady Jun passed away. She was Shengzi. Since no announcement was sent to the feudal lords, no mourning was held in the ancestral temple, and no ancestral tablet was placed in the ancestral shrine, she was not referred to as having "died" (hong). She was not called "Lady" (furen), so her burial was not recorded. Her surname was not recorded because of the Duke, so she was called "Lady Jun."
○Duke Wu of Zheng and Duke Zhuang served as ministers to King Ping. The King favored Guo, which caused the Earl of Zheng to resent the King. The King said, "That is not so." Thus, Zhou and Zheng exchanged hostages. Prince Hu of Zhou was held hostage in Zheng, and Prince Hu of Zheng was held hostage in Zhou. When the King passed away, the people of Zhou were about to give governmental authority to the Duke of Guo. In the fourth month, Ji Zu of Zheng led troops to harvest the wheat of Wen. In autumn, they again harvested the grain of Chengzhou. Zhou and Zheng became hostile to each other.
The noble man said: "If trust is not sincere from the heart, hostages are of no use. If one acts with understanding and forbearance, binding oneself with propriety, even without hostages, who can cause discord?" If there is clear sincerity, even the grass of streams and marshes, the vegetables of duckweed and algae, the vessels of baskets and cauldrons, the water of pools and ditches, can be offered to spirits and gods, and can be presented to kings and dukes. How much more so when noble men establish trust between two states and act with propriety—what need is there for hostages? The Airs contain "Gathering Duckweed" and "Gathering Water Plants," and the Elegantiae contain "Walking on the Reeds" and "Drawing from a Distance," all manifesting loyalty and trust."
○A son of the Wu family came to request contributions for the funeral, as the King had not yet been buried.
○Duke Mu of Song was ill, so he summoned the Grand Marshal Kong Fu and entrusted Duke Shang to him, saying: "The former ruler set aside Yuyi and established me. I dare not forget this. If through the blessings of the great officers, I am able to preserve my position until death, when the former ruler asks about Yuyi, what words shall I use to respond? I ask you to support him and make him the master of the altars of state. Though I die, I will have no regrets." Kong Fu replied: "The ministers all wish to support Feng." The Duke said: "That cannot be. The former ruler considered me worthy and made me master of the altars. If I abandon virtue and do not yield, that would be to nullify the former ruler's decision. How could I then be called worthy? To illuminate and carry forward the former ruler's excellent virtue—should I not strive for this? I ask you not to nullify the former ruler's achievement." He then sent Prince Feng to reside in Zheng. In the eighth month, on the day Gengchen, Duke Mu of Song passed away, and Duke Shang ascended the throne.
The noble man said: "Duke Xuan of Song may be said to have known people well. He established Duke Mu, and his son enjoyed the fruits of it. This was a command of righteousness. The Shang Hymns say: 'Yin received the mandate, all was fitting; a hundred blessings were borne.' Is this not what is meant?"
○Winter, Qi and Zheng made a covenant at Shimen, renewing the covenant of Lu. On the day Gengxu, the Earl of Zheng's chariot overturned in the Ji River.
○Duke Zhuang of Wei married the younger sister of Dechen, the heir of Qi, named Zhuang Jiang. She was beautiful but had no sons, which is why the people of Wei composed the poem "Shuo Ren." He also married a woman from Chen, named Li Gui, who gave birth to Xiao Bo, who died early. Her younger sister Dai Gui gave birth to Duke Huan, and Zhuang Jiang treated him as her own son. Prince Zhouyu was the son of a favored concubine. ○He was favored and fond of military affairs. The Duke did not restrain him, and Zhuang Jiang detested him. Shi Que admonished, saying: "I have heard that one who loves his son teaches him with righteousness and does not lead him into evil. Arrogance, extravagance, licentiousness, and dissipation are the paths to evil. These arise from excessive favor and honor. If you intend to establish Zhouyu, then settle the matter; if not, you will be creating disaster step by step. Those who are favored but not arrogant, arrogant but able to humble themselves, humbled but not resentful, resentful but able to restrain themselves—such people are rare. Moreover, the lowly obstructing the noble, the young overriding the elder, the distant alienating the close, the new displacing the old, the small exceeding the great, and licentiousness breaking righteousness—these are called the six perversions. The ruler righteous, the minister obedient, the father kind, the son filial, the elder brother loving, the younger brother respectful—these are called the six conformities. To abandon conformity and imitate perversion is to hasten disaster. One who rules over others should strive to remove disaster, but to hasten it—is that not unacceptable?" The Duke did not listen. His son Hou associated with Zhouyu, and he tried to stop him but could not. When Duke Huan was established, Shi Que retired due to old age.

【Classic】
Year 4, Spring, in the King's second month, the people of Ju attacked Qi and took Moulou.
○On the day Wushen, Zhouyu of Wei assassinated his ruler Wan.
○Summer, the Duke met with the Duke of Song at Qing.
○The Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the people of Cai, and the people of Wei attacked Zheng.
○Autumn, Hui led troops to join the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the people of Cai, and the people of Wei in attacking Zheng.
○In the ninth month, the people of Wei killed Zhouyu at Pu.
○Winter, in the twelfth month, the people of Wei established Jin.
【Commentary】
Year 4, Spring, Zhouyu of Wei assassinated Duke Huan and established himself.
○The Duke and the Duke of Song held a meeting, intending to renew the covenant of Su. Before the appointed time, the people of Wei came to report the disorder.
○Summer, the Duke met with the Duke of Song at Qing.
○When Duke Shang of Song ascended the throne, Prince Feng fled to Zheng, and the people of Zheng wanted to restore him. When Zhouyu of Wei was established, he sought to avenge the former ruler's grievances against Zheng and to gain favor with the feudal lords in order to pacify his people. He sent a message to Song, saying: "If you, my lord, attack Zheng to remove your own harm, with you as the leader, our humble state will follow with Chen and Cai with our resources—this would be the wish of Wei." The people of Song agreed. At that time, Chen and Cai were on good terms with Wei, so the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the people of Cai, and the people of Wei attacked Zheng, besieging its East Gate, and returned after five days.
The Duke asked Zhong Zhong: "Will Zhouyu of Wei succeed?" He replied: "I have heard of harmonizing the people through virtue, not through disorder. To use disorder is like trying to untangle silk by tangling it further. As for Zhouyu, he relies on military force and is content with cruelty. Relying on force, he will have no followers; content with cruelty, he will have no kin. When the people rebel and kin are alienated, success is difficult. Military force is like fire; if not extinguished, it will burn itself. Zhouyu assassinated his ruler and harshly used his people. Not striving for excellent virtue but wishing to succeed through disorder—he will certainly not escape disaster."
○Autumn, the feudal lords again attacked Zheng. The Duke of Song sent a messenger to request troops, but the Duke declined. Yufu requested to lead troops to join, but the Duke did not permit. He insisted and went. Therefore, the text says "Hui led troops," expressing disapproval of him. The allied troops defeated Zheng's infantry, took their grain, and returned.
○Zhouyu was unable to harmonize his people. Hou asked Shi Que about how to settle the ruler. Shi Que said: "An audience with the King would be appropriate." Hou asked: "How can we obtain an audience?" He replied: "Duke Huan of Chen is currently favored by the King, and Chen and Wei are on good terms. If you go to court with Chen and request it, it will certainly be granted." Hou followed Zhouyu to Chen. Shi Que sent word to Chen, saying: "The state of Wei is small, and I am old and feeble, unable to act. These two men truly assassinated our ruler. I dare to ask you to deal with them immediately." The people of Chen seized them and requested that Wei send someone to execute them. In the ninth month, the people of Wei sent You Zai Chou to Pu to execute Zhouyu, and Shi Que sent his steward Niu Yangjian to Chen to execute Shi Hou.
The noble man said: "Shi Que was a loyal minister. He detested Zhouyu and thus Hou was implicated. 'Great righteousness extinguishes kinship'—is this not what is meant?"
The people of Wei welcomed Prince Jin from Xing. Winter, in the twelfth month, Duke Xuan ascended the throne. The text says "the people of Wei established Jin," meaning it was the will of the multitude.

【Classic】
Year 5, Spring, the Duke went to view fish at Tang.
○Summer, in the fourth month, Duke Huan of Wei was buried.
○Autumn, the Wei army entered Cheng.
○In the ninth month, the temple of Zhongzi was completed, and for the first time six rows of feather dancers were offered.
○The people of Zhu and the people of Zheng attacked Song.
○There were locusts.
○Winter, in the twelfth month, on the day Xinsi, Prince Wan passed away.
○The people of Song attacked Zheng and besieged Changge.
【Commentary】
Year 5, Spring, the Duke was about to go to Tang to view fish. Zang Xibo admonished, saying: "If things are not sufficient for discussing great affairs, and their materials are not sufficient for preparing implements, then the ruler should not act upon them. The ruler is one who leads the people into proper standards and things. Therefore, discussing affairs to measure standards is called 'standards'; taking materials to display the colors of things is called 'things.' What is not standard and not proper is called 'disorderly governance.' When disorderly governance is frequently practiced, it leads to ruin. Therefore, the spring hunt, summer hunt, autumn hunt, and winter hunt are all conducted in the leisure of agriculture to discuss affairs. Every three years, troops are drilled; upon return, the army is reviewed; upon return, a feast is held to count the military achievements. Displaying insignia, clarifying noble and base, distinguishing ranks, following the order of young and old—these are for practicing majesty and ceremony. The flesh of birds and beasts that does not go onto the sacrificial stands, and the hides, teeth, bones, horns, and feathers that do not go onto implements—the Duke does not shoot them. This is the ancient system. As for the products of mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes, the resources for implements, the tasks of servants, and the duties of officials—these are not matters for the ruler." The Duke said: "I will inspect the territory." He then went, displayed the fish, and viewed them. Xibo claimed illness and did not follow. The text says "the Duke went to view fish at Tang," which was against propriety, and also notes it was a distant place.
○Zhuang Bo of Quwo, with the people of Zheng and Xing, attacked Yi. The King sent Yin Shi and Wu Shi to assist them. The Marquis of Yi fled to Sui.
○Summer, Duke Huan of Wei was buried. Because of the disorder in Wei, the burial was delayed.
○In the fourth month, the people of Zheng invaded the pastures of Wei, to avenge the battle of the East Gate. The people of Wei, with the Yan army, attacked Zheng. Ji Zu, Yuan Fan, and Xie Jia of Zheng stationed three armies in front, and sent Man Bo and Zi Yuan to secretly station troops behind. The Yan people feared Zheng's three armies but did not anticipate the people of Zhi. In the sixth month, the two princes of Zheng, with the people of Zhi, defeated the Yan army at Beizhi.
The noble man said: "If one does not prepare for the unexpected, one cannot lead troops."
○Quwo rebelled against the King. In autumn, the King ordered the Duke of Guo to attack Quwo and established Marquis Ai at Yi.
○During the disorder in Wei, the people of Cheng invaded Wei, so the Wei army entered Cheng.
○In the ninth month, the temple of Zhongzi was completed, and they were about to perform the wan dance. The Duke asked Zhong Zhong about the number of feather dancers. He replied: "The Son of Heaven uses eight rows, the feudal lords six, the great officers four, and the officers two. Dance is used to regulate the eight sounds and spread the eight winds, so it goes from eight downward." The Duke followed this. Thus, for the first time six rows of feather dancers were offered, beginning the use of six yi.
○The people of Song took the fields of Zhu. The people of Zhu told Zheng: "We ask you, my lord, to vent your grievances against Song; our humble state will serve as the guide." The people of Zheng, with the King's army, joined them, attacked Song, and entered its outer wall, to avenge the battle of the East Gate. The people of Song sent a messenger with orders. The Duke heard that they had entered the outer wall and was about to rescue them. He asked the messenger: "How far has the army reached?" He replied: "It has not yet reached the capital." The Duke was angry and stopped. He declined the messenger, saying: "Your ruler commanded me to share in the troubles of the altars of state. Now I asked the messenger, and he said 'the army has not yet reached the capital.' This is not something I dare to know about."
○Winter, in the twelfth month, on the day Xinsi, Zang Xibo passed away. The Duke said: "My uncle had grievances against me, and I dare not forget them." He buried him with one rank higher.
○The people of Song attacked Zheng and besieged Changge, to avenge the battle of entering the outer wall.

"A good man is blameless, but his jade will bring him ruin."

Grandfather... or rather, our Grand Master, told me something before he departed on his final pilgrimage. He said that in the year of the cup-offering ceremony, our workshop laid no profane hand upon the Night Brightness jade. How could we? How could those who live to bring forth the soul of jade be the ones to corrupt it? The truth is, the massacre was born from a vicious power struggle among the Bodchen. They made our cup a vessel for their poison, and our craftsmen the sacrifice for their schemes. Every carver on Crystal Shore had their arms severed. Every one of them perished.

This is why Grandfather's last words to me were a warning, etched in blood: stay far away from the games of power. General Zhang Huaishen may be kind and approachable now, but you must hold this truth in your heart: artisans and nobles must never mix. Otherwise, the tragedy of the tribute cup will surely befall us again.

zh:
公主悬赏凉州十景诗的消息传遍了所有的村落，茅屋中的少年兴奋地举起未干的诗稿。
他兴冲冲地骑上小毛驴，沿着山道，向那位公主的高塔走去。
驴儿似乎感受到了主人的欢乐，咴咴地叫着。
“驴兄，驴兄，我就要发达了！”他举起自己的诗稿，“我的大作一定能得到公主的赏识！”

望帝乡前，少年捧着落选的诗稿，和那一两黄金出神。
公主朱批：字词朴拙，跳脱韵律，但情意流露，足见赤诚，当赏金一两。
少年有些不可置信，但仍跨上毛驴，奔着天水集而去。
有了这一两黄金，他便和窣利人学起了做生意，逐渐成为一方巨贾。

多年后，他的车队再次返回凉州。途径玉露台，他仿佛看到了当年骑着毛驴献诗的自己。
他再次提笔，写下《凉州十一景》。他绞尽脑汁用尽笔墨，描摹公主的绝代风华，称其为凉州第十一道绝景。笔落诗成，他满意地将诗封于金匮，连同财宝一起献给住在望帝乡中的公主。
不多时，望帝乡中走出一列宫娥，为首的那位将财宝与金阙原封不动交还于商人。只是金匮之上，多了一两黄金，和一道朱批。

公主朱批：矢志诗文，赏金一两。然吾仍爱君初献之作。
en:
News that the princess was offering a reward for poems about the Ten Scenes of Liangzhou spread to all villages. A young man in a thatched cottage excitedly held up his still-damp manuscript. 
He happily mounted his small donkey and walked along the mountain path toward the princess's tall tower. 
The donkey seemed to feel its master's joy and brayed cheerfully. 
"Brother Donkey, Brother Donkey, I'm going to make it big!" He held up his manuscript, "My masterpiece will surely win the princess's appreciation!" 

In front of the Homesight Tower, the young man stared blankly at his rejected manuscript and the tael of gold. 
The princess's red annotation read: "The words are simple and lack rhythm, but they reveal sincere feelings. A reward of one tael of gold is granted." 
The young man couldn't believe it, but he still mounted his donkey and raced toward Skybrim Market. 
With this tael of gold, he learned to do business from the Sogdians and gradually became a wealthy merchant. 

Many years later, his caravan returned to Liangzhou. Passing the Cleardew Terrace, he seemed to see his younger self riding the small donkey to present his poem. 
He picked up his brush again and wrote "The Eleventh Scene of Liangzhou." He racked his brains and used all his literary skills to depict the princess's peerless beauty, calling her the eleventh magnificent scene of Liangzhou. When he finished writing, he happily sealed the poem in a golden casket and presented it to the princess living in the Homesight Tower, along with treasures. 
Soon after, a line of palace maids walked out of the tower. The leader returned the treasures and the golden casket to the merchant intact. Only on the golden casket were an additional tael of gold and another red annotation. 

The princess's red annotation read: "You are dedicated to poetry, another tael of gold as a reward. Yet I still love your original submission."

zh:
游侠如晤：

近日寒暑不定，不知你在外奔走，饮食起居可还妥帖？

出门在外，传信不易。几次想写信问你近况，又怕信送到时，你已去了别处。倒是昨日在聆杏村遇着一桩巧事，说与你听听。

我碰见一位同门，不仅长相与我九分相似，连名字都一模一样，也唤“石惊天”。更奇者，他所言之挚友，竟也出身清河，似乎是名唤$C$L#Y$PN#E$C。

天下虽大，这般巧合却也难得，想来也唯有”缘分“二字才可解释。

那位石兄说，他这几日路过医馆好几回，每次都想进去向青溪弟子讨教些医术，却始终没迈进门槛。

我问他为何突然想学医。他说，家中友人常年在外行侠，也常涉险地，不是动骨扭挫，就是身染疫瘴，每每带伤返归，他都揪心不已，若也能学些岐黄之道，或可替其分忧一二。

一番推心，到底同门，石某脸皮厚些，便替他往医馆跑一趟。若是于医术有所进益，往后你若也不慎受伤，便可寻我医治。

若归期稍晚，还望游侠勿要挂念。

石惊天
en:
To the Wanderer:
The weather has been unpredictable lately. Are you eating and resting well on your travels?
Sending letters while traveling is not easy. I wanted to write and ask how you were several times, but feared you would have already moved on by the time the letter arrived. However, I encountered a coincidence in Apricot Village yesterday that I must tell you about.
I met a fellow disciple who not only looks quite like me but also shares the exact same name, "Shi Jingtian." Even more bizarrely, the close friend he mentioned also hails from Qinghe and seems to be named $C$L#Y$PN#E$C.
Though the world is vast, such coincidences are rare. I suppose only "destiny" can explain it.
This Brother Shi said he had passed by the clinic several times over the past few days. Each time, he wanted to go in and ask the Silver Needle disciples for medical advice but never crossed the threshold.
I asked him why he suddenly wanted to learn medicine. He said his friend is always out being a hero, often venturing into dangerous places, resulting in sprains, fractures, or diseases. Every time his friend returns injured, his heart aches. He thought if he could learn some healing arts, he could share some of the burden.
After a heart-to-heart, since we are fellow disciples, I decided to be thick-skinned and run to the clinic for him. If I can improve my medical skills, then if you ever get injured, you can come to me for treatment.
If my return is slightly delayed, please do not worry, Wanderer.
Shi Jingtian

zh:
麦香客栈的店小二已经是第三天见到这个背着背篓的小姑娘了。

小姑娘每日来了便坐在门边，望着街上，吹来一阵风，她就禁不住要咳嗽两声，可怜见的，像她背篓里那消瘦的小猫似的。
“你天天望着那街上，是在望什么？”小二终于忍不住问。
“我在等一个人。”那小姑娘笑嘻嘻答。
“你不知道他啥时候来吗？”
“知道……也不知道。”她托着腮嘟囔着，路口忽然传来了争执之声，她向外望去，忽的嫣然一笑——“来了！”话音未落，她便像一只蝴蝶似的飞了出去。

小二也忙探头看，只看到一个愣头愣脑的侠客，竟然碰了无忧帮的硬茬。
“就等这人啊……还不如等我呢。”小二撇撇嘴。
en:
The Wheatwind Inn's waiter had seen the little girl with the bamboo basket for three straight days.

Each day, she'd sit by the door, staring down the street. When the wind blew, she'd cough softly, delicate as the skinny kitten in her basket.
"What're you staring at out there all day?" he finally asked.
"I'm waiting for someone," she chirped, grinning.
"Don't you know when they'll come?"
"I do... and I don't." She rested her chin in her hand. Just then, a commotion erupted at the crossroads. She looked out and smiled radiantly.
 "There he is!" Before the words fell, she flitted out like a butterfly.

The waiter craned his neck to see: just a clumsy-looking swordsman had stumbled into the Unbound Cavern's territory.
"Waiting for that guy... might as well wait for me," the waiter muttered, clicking his tongue.

zh:
兰守持以为是女儿离家太久，忘记了自己的鞋履尺寸。
但快乐的他来不及找鞋垫子，就穿着这宽松的鞋，脚下生风地前去赴女儿的约。

直到最后他才明白，这鞋就是他曾经的尺寸。
而现在他老了。
人老了，雄心壮志缩了水。高大身材也在日复一日的鞠躬中，瘦了下来小了下来。
但女儿记得的，还是他曾经的大脚。

他抱着年幼的女儿去求医，那武林名宿的山门紧紧闭着。他等了很久，甚至一瞬间，膝盖就要跪下去。他跪了吗？有什么让他犹豫了吗？膝盖在疼，是皎皎在叫他吗？皎皎当时说什么来着？
兰守持一边想着，一边拍打着巨石，他想到了，皎皎说——
“我的爹爹是惊涛掌，是这世间一等一的大英雄。”
皎皎说，我是大英雄呐。
兰守持一掌拍了出去。
巨石裂开。
半掌惊涛，重现江湖。

在这无人在意的，尸体堆里。
en:
Lan Shouchi assumed his daughter had been away from home too long and forgotten his shoe size.
Overjoyed, he had no time to find insoles. He wore the loose shoes and rushed to meet his daughter with a spring in his step.

Only at the very end did he realize the shoes were precisely his former size.
But he had grown old.
With age, lofty ambitions shrank. His tall stature had withered and diminished through daily bowing and scraping.
Yet his daughter still remembered him with large feet.

He carried his young daughter to seek a doctor, but the famous martial artist's gates were tightly shut. He waited a long time. For a moment, his knees nearly hit the ground. Did he kneel? What made him hesitate? His knees hurt. Was Jiaojiao calling him? What did Jiaojiao say back then?
As Lan Shouchi pondered, he struck the massive boulder. He remembered. Jiaojiao said—
"My father is the Palm Strike Master, a paramount hero of this world."
Jiaojiao said I am a great hero.
Lan Shouchi struck with his palm.
The massive boulder cracked.
Half‑Palm Against the Tide re-emerged in the Jianghu.

Here, in a pile of corpses nobody cared about.

Later, an eminent monk who beheld this mirror sighed and said: "This is no common object—when the moment of fate arrives, it shall of itself return to its former brilliance." It seems this mirror, connecting yin and yang, perhaps seeks to glimpse once more, in the narrow gap between life and death, the face of its former master.

弦是断的，琴宫是缺的，如此回溯旧案，伤筋动骨。
在送走郑生之后，麦陵野人终于应允唐新词所求，将此物传给她。
一代人总有一代人的路要走，有想知道的真相要查。

This string is said to have once belonged to Daozhen's lineage. By the time Wheat Ridge Recluse acquired it, it had long since snapped into several pieces and could no longer produce a pure note.
The string is broken, the Gong-Note Zither incomplete. Reconstructing an old case this way is a painful undertaking.
After seeing Zheng Sheng off, Wheat Ridge Recluse finally granted Tang Xinci's request and passed the string to her.
Every generation has its own road to walk and its own truths to seek.
Yet now it seems this broken string was briefly joined by the Harmonizer, and someone entered by mistake.
Such is timing; such is fate. At last, the "Gong-Note Zither" of Mount Tai Blizzard has a string that answers.

Qu Yuan once said: "I would rather cast myself into the Xiang River and rest within the bellies of river fish." Yet white steeds were cast into the surging waters, and with them the pure-hearted scholars perished. The dead are gone, yet the living dream on.
The past feels like yesterday while rain pours without pause. Even without a Pillow of Yellow Millet, one may still call back the souls of the departed. In dreams, deep pools and still waters cannot hide that lingering fragrance. Though spring has withered away, daylight shines bright once more.

To $N,

Your letter has been received. The relevant leads are as follows:
Zhen Sheji, formerly a disciple of the Inkbound Order. For years he was consumed by the writing of storybooks, determined to set down the injustices of the world. Yet his work was too sharp, too close to what was real, and for a long while found no favor with buyers or readers alike.
He lived in straitened circumstances, burdened by debt. In matters of writing he was stubborn to the point of obsession, and often quarreled fiercely with his fellow disciples, both senior and junior. In the end, he left without a word and stormed off in anger.

He was last seen wandering the jianghu, seemingly gathering clues on all sides for an old murder case in Kaifeng. The dead man in that case was called Shen Mo.

The waning moon casts light on a lone shadow; drifting sand muffles ghostly cries.
Along the endless road, sand surges to the sky, the moon shrouded in darkness. Amid the windswept dunes, only scattered remnants linger, unable to depart.

zh:
青州伽蓝记·早悟寺 
早悟寺者，在泰山之东阴，大泊之阳，山水辉映，实为幽境。寺本名枣核，唐贞元中所立也。
昔青州有民陈氏，名讳不考，世居临淄。贞元初，随父商贾，贩枣彭城。货既毕，父遘疾，殒于归途。自后孤苦无依，悲恸不能自已，叹曰："人生如寄，聚散无常。父以枣利而亡，儿以枣故而孤，此非天意乎？"遂落发为僧，遁迹空门。
乡人闻之，莫不惋惜。有长者议曰："陈氏父子之悲剧，岂独一家哉？后世孤儿失怙者，将何所归？"乃相率捐资，于泰山下立小刹，名曰枣核寺。寺成，收容孤幼，给以衣食，教以经书。自是之后，无家之子，皆有所归。
寺临山傍水，古木参天，曲径通幽。中有禅房数楹，形制虽朴，巧构难加。禅阁虚静，隐室凝邃。嘉树夹牖，芳杜匝阶。春鸟秋蝉，鸣声相续。虽处尘世，想同岩谷。静行之僧，绳坐其内，餐风服道，结跏数息。
寺后有古枣树一株，传为陈氏父子所植。岁久干粗，枝叶繁衍，子实甚大。枣熟之时，寺僧采而分之，孤幼得食，皆感佛恩。
后历五代，寺渐倾颓，其所纳幼童与僧众皆还俗。至宋初，有文津馆弟子数人，游学至此。见寺中有缁衣僧人居住，复有黄冠道者挂名其间，佛道杂处，各修其法。弟子谓众曰："此山灵秀，实为三教共修之地。"有比丘道觉者云："不若改称早悟，广纳儒释道三家。渡天下之黎民者，岂独伽蓝？参往昔之福祸者，无非早悟。"众皆称善，遂易名为早悟寺。
又闻民间有棉花娘娘者，护佑织纺，泽被黎庶。乡老请入寺中，立祠奉祀。自是佛殿道观儒堂并列，香火益盛，信徒辐辏。
寺东有洞天一处，乃道家修真之所。入洞仅十步，有幽石垂树，虽芥子之地亦有洞天之渺。洞中幽深，虽炎夏而凉气袭人。有道士，修炼其中，服气导引，不问世事。洞中古藤缠绕，野花丛生，鸟雀时鸣，真仙境也。
今寺隐密林之中，人迹罕至。晨钟暮鼓，声闻数里。登寺远眺，大泊如镜，泰山如屏。烟波浩渺，峰峦叠翠。
嗟乎！世事无常，盛衰有数。昔日椿萱之悲，今为早悟之慈。一寺之名，几经更易，而慈悲之心，历久弥坚。三教共融，各得其妙，此乃泰山之灵秀所钟也。后人游此，当思人生苦短，及早觉悟，勿待白发方悔少年时也。
en:
From the Record of Buddhist Monasteries: Seedling Temple.

Seedling Temple rests on the eastern shade of Mount Tai and the sunny northern shore of the Great Lake. Reflected in the mountain and water, it is truly a realm of serenity. The temple was originally named Jujube Pit, established during the Zhenyuan era of the Tang Dynasty.
In the past, there was a commoner of Qingzhou surnamed Chen, his given name lost to time, whose family had lived in Linzi for generations. In the early Zhenyuan era, he followed his merchant father to sell jujubes in Pengcheng. After the goods were sold, his father contracted an illness and perished on the journey home. Left orphaned and helpless, the son was overcome with inconsolable grief. He sighed, "Life is but a fleeting lodging; meetings and partings are impermanent. My father died for the profit of jujubes, and I am orphaned because of jujubes. Is this not the will of Heaven?" He then shaved his head to become a monk, vanishing into the Buddhist gates.
Upon hearing this, the local villagers were filled with pity. A village elder remarked, "Is the tragedy of the Chen family truly isolated? Where shall the orphaned children of future generations find refuge?" Thus, they pooled their funds and built a small sanctuary at the foot of Mount Tai, naming it Jujube Pit Temple. Once completed, it took in orphans, providing them with food, clothing, and the teachings of the scriptures. From then on, the homeless children of the land had a place to return to.
The temple sits by the mountains and waters, shaded by towering ancient trees, with winding paths leading to profound seclusion. Within are several meditation halls; though simple in form, their craftsmanship is exquisite. The zen pavilions are empty and quiet, the hidden chambers deep and still. Splendid trees line the windows, and fragrant herbs encircle the steps. Spring birds and autumn cicadas sing in succession. Though situated in the mortal realm, it feels akin to a deep ravine. Monks of quiet practice sit upright inside, living on the wind and the Dao, settling into lotus posture to count their breaths.
Behind the temple stands an ancient jujube tree, said to have been planted by the Chen father and son. Over the years, its trunk has grown thick, its branches flourishing, yielding massive fruits. When the jujubes ripen, the monks harvest and distribute them. The orphans who eat them all feel gratitude for the Buddha's grace.
Passing through the Five Dynasties, the temple gradually fell into ruin, and the children and monks it sheltered returned to secular life. In the early Song Dynasty, several disciples of the Inkbound Order arrived here on their academic travels. They saw dark-robed Buddhist monks residing in the temple, alongside yellow-capped Daoist priests who also registered their names there. Buddhists and Daoists mingled, each practicing their own way. The disciples told the crowd, "This mountain is imbued with spiritual grace; it is truly a place for the Three Teachings to cultivate together." A monk named Daojue said, "Why not rename it 'Seedling' (Dawn of Enlightenment), to broadly embrace Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism? Are the monasteries the only ones who save the common people? To contemplate the blessings and misfortunes of the past is nothing but an early awakening." All praised the idea, and the name was changed to Seedling Temple.
Later, hearing of the Cotton Goddess among the folk, who protects weavers and blesses the commoners, the village elders invited her shrine into the temple. Since then, Buddhist halls, Daoist shrines, and Confucian academies stand side by side. The incense burns ever brighter, and believers gather like spokes to a hub.
East of the temple lies a hidden grotto, a place for Daoist cultivation. Just ten steps inside, shadowed stones and drooping trees reveal a profound realm, a universe hidden within a mustard seed. The cave is deep and secluded; even in the blazing summer, a chilling breeze strikes the skin. A Daoist priest cultivates within, guiding his breath and absorbing the essence, ignoring worldly affairs. Ancient vines entwine the cave, wildflowers bloom in clusters, and birds chirp occasionally. It is a true immortal paradise.
Today, the temple is hidden within a dense forest, rarely visited by men. Yet the morning bell and evening drum resound for miles. Ascending the temple to gaze afar, the Great Lake is like a mirror, and Mount Tai like a screen. The misty waters are boundless, the emerald peaks layered.
Alas! The affairs of the world are impermanent, and prosperity and decline have their destined times. The grief of losing one's parents in the past has transformed into the mercy of Seedling Temple today. The name of a single temple has changed multiple times, yet its heart of compassion has only grown firmer through the ages. The Three Teachings blend together, each attaining its own wonder; this is the spiritual focus of Mount Tai. Future generations who visit here should reflect on the brevity of life and seek enlightenment early, lest they wait until their hair turns white to regret the days of their youth.

zh:
寒姨说过，骰子这玩意儿，碰不得。
少东家不明白，只心痒得难受，可$T(30)转念一想，寒姨做事，向来有她的章法。而自己是要当大侠的人，这点“忍”字功夫，算得了什么？
可人群围着骰子叫好的场景，却总在$T(30)念书、练剑的间隙，悄悄浮上心头。
直到一日夜里，少东家做了个怪梦——自己竟变成了一粒骰子，在众人的喝彩声里，在桌案上滴溜溜地转个不停。
那喝彩越响，$T(30)转得越欢。可转完了，$T(30)心头却越空落落的……在那些时刻，仿佛得了他们的喝彩，自己才是个好的骰子。
蓦地惊醒，少东家的背心已沁出一层薄汗。窗外月色清明，$T(30)长长舒了口气： “寒姨说的，果然没错。”
en:
Aunt Han always said the same thing: stay away from dice.
The Young Master never really understood why. If anything, the warning only made him more curious. Still, Aunt Han always did things for a reason. And if $T(30) was going to become a hero one day, then a little self-control was to be expected.
Even so, the sound of people crowding around the dice table, shouting and cheering, kept creeping back into $T(30)'s mind between lessons and sword practice.
Then one night, he had a strange dream. He dreamed he had turned into a die, spinning across the table while the crowd roared around him.
The louder they cheered, the faster $T(30) spun. But once it stopped, all he felt was empty. It was as though their cheers were the only thing that made him worth anything.
He woke with a start, a thin layer of sweat on his back. The moonlight outside was clear and cold. $T(30) let out a long breath. "Aunt Han was right after all."

zh:
编钟，我国古代青铜打击乐器，兴起于周代，盛行于春秋战国至秦汉时期，是礼乐文明的重要象征。
编钟由若干个大小不同的钟，按音调高低，有序地悬挂于木制钟架之上，通过丁字形木槌和长棒敲击发声。
编钟的钟体小，音调便高，音量也小；钟体大，音调则低，音量也大。
en:
The bianzhong is an ancient Chinese percussion instrument that emerged during the Zhou dynasty and flourished from the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods through the Qin and Han dynasties. It was an important symbol of China's ritual and musical traditions.

A bianzhong set consists of a series of bells in different sizes, arranged according to pitch and suspended in order on a wooden frame. They are played by striking with T-shaped wooden mallets and long sticks.

Smaller bells produce higher pitches and softer sounds, while larger bells produce deeper tones and greater volume.

云华楼静雅清幽，如芳草佳人，朝饮木兰之坠露，夕餐秋菊之落英。小楼二三层，以雕花雪纸、芙蓉香兰点缀窗帐。偶有琴音随花香泄出，其声悠悠然，不过三两声，便足以推皱楼外池水，以涟漪三千，照映斜晖脉脉。
文人骚客深爱之，常于楼内小聚。或曲水流觞，吟诗作对良辰；或舞雩修禊，歌叹陌上青春。弱兰或沏香煮雪汀岸，或抚琴吹萧凭栏，若有美一人，解语水中央。
en:
The Velvet Shade featured two famous girls: Zhou Qiang of Revelry Hall, and Ruolan of Nimbus Tower. 
Nimbus Tower was quiet and remote, like a beautiful flower that drank the morning dew and dined on fallen petals. It had three floors, each decorated with paper cuttings and fragrant incense. Occasionally the sound of a guqin sent ripples across the pond, with the setting sun gazing down from the sky. 
The scholars often gathered at Nimbus Tower or the rivers nearby to write poems, dance, or sing. Ruolan made tea or played instruments, and everything revolved around her beauty.

言念蠲豆笾之荐，聿修宗事之严；蹈天志之向，共以素风之旧。
十五年之莫逆，岂止青梅之交。四千日长怀慕，敢有婚姻之请。
盛事衣冠，既婚姻之是托。百年琴瑟，庶茀履以咸宜。

en:
I, Su Qizhe of Hidden Mountain, bow in respect and humbly pray for your consent.
In keeping with the proper rites of ancestral offering and the solemn duties of the family, and in the hope of joining two houses in the spirit of long held virtue and shared values, I now make this request in all sincerity.
For fifteen years, we have shared a bond of rare closeness, far beyond the fond companionship of childhood. Through these four thousand days, admiration has been cherished in my heart, and so at last I dare to speak of marriage.
This is a matter of great joy and solemn meaning. If this union may be entrusted to your favor, then may we spend a lifetime together in harmony, and may every step we take together be blessed and fitting.
The omens have already been consulted and found auspicious. I now present this letter and the wedding goose in earnest, to make known my sincerity.
With humble respect, I await your honored reply, and ask that you look kindly upon this proposal.
14th day of the ninth month, fifth year of Xiande,
Formal marriage proposal submitted by Su Qizhe.

zh:
菜菜生在开封，长在开封，是一只地地道道的开封猫。
它曾是开封街头最厉害的小霸王，黑蛋儿则是它最忠诚的小跟班。它们俩一个负责偷，一个负责抢，合作无间。直到那天，它们啃到了一根硬骨头。
那天，菜菜在升平桥旁巡视，看上了一个胖大汉手里的肉饼，指挥黑蛋儿上前佯攻，自己绕后叼走肉饼。没想到那大汉不躲不闪，只用脚轻轻一绊，黑蛋儿就摔了个狗啃泥，还顺手拎起了正欲逃跑的菜菜。看着剧烈挣扎的一猫一狗，这大汉不生气，反而蹲下来，饶有兴致地看着它们：“噫！瞧瞧这俩孩儿，一个撺掇事儿，一个还真敢上，怪得劲儿的嘞！ ”
他把肉饼掰了一半，一半给了呜咽的黑蛋儿，另一半递到菜菜面前。黑蛋儿不吃，都咬给了菜菜，而菜菜则警惕地看着这大汉——这人身上有股说不出的气势。见黑蛋儿和菜菜都不吃，大汉笑道：“咋嘞？还怕俺在这饼里头下药？ ”
看着这一猫一狗紧张害怕，却又相互回护的样子，大汉又不由笑道：“中！恁俩跟俺当年那些弟兄们可像嘞，都讲义气。” 
从那天起，这人就时常来街上找它们，有时带吃的，有时就看它们玩闹。后来有一天，菜菜和黑蛋儿跟着他一路走，不知道咋的就走进了一处干净漂亮的地方，墙很高很高，人也很多很多，从此，它们就在这里住下了。
这里有吃不完的饭，抓不完的胖鲤鱼，菜菜和黑蛋儿每天都有数不清的游戏可以玩儿。大汉偶尔散步路过池边时，也总喜欢看着菜菜和黑蛋儿，感叹道：“唉，还得是恁这些小玩意儿活得舒坦。哪儿像俺呐，反倒不如以前快活嘞。”
菜菜听不懂这汉子说的话，但菜菜知道，这里有饭吃，有鱼摸，还有黑蛋儿一起玩儿，就是全天下最好最好的地方！
en:
Veggie was born in Kaifeng and grew up in Kaifeng, a true local cat through and through.

Back on the streets, it was the toughest little bully around. Heidan was its most loyal sidekick. One did the stealing, the other did the snatching. Together, they were unstoppable.

Until one day, they picked the wrong target.

Veggie was prowling near Harmonic Span when it spotted a meat pie in the hands of a big, burly man. Veggie had Heidan rush in as a distraction while it looped around behind to make off with the pie.

The man did not even dodge.
He simply hooked a foot out. Heidan went down face-first, and the man caught Veggie with the same easy motion as if it weighed nothing.

The cat and dog fought like mad in his grip. The man did not get angry. He crouched down instead, studying them with amused interest.

"Well now. Would you look at you two."
"One starts the trouble, and the other actually goes for it. That's something."

He split the pie in half. One piece went to the whimpering Heidan other he held out in front of Veggie.

Heidan would not eat. It pushed its share toward Veggie with its nose.
Veggie, however, stared at the man warily. There was something about him that put it on edge.

Seeing neither of them bite, the man laughed.

"What, you think I put something in it?"

They were scared stiff, yet still trying to shield each other. The man laughed again, softer this time.

"Fine. You two remind me of my old brothers. Loyal to the bone."

After that, the man kept showing up. Sometimes he brought food. Sometimes he just watched them roughhouse.

Then one day, Veggie and Heidan followed him for a long while. Somehow, they ended up in a place that was clean and beautiful, with walls so high and crowds so thick it made Veggie's head spin.

And that was where they stayed.

There was food that never ran out, fat carp to catch, and more games than they could count.

When the man strolled past the pond now, he would often pause to watch them and sigh.

"Yeah. You little rascals have it good."
"Me? I'm not half as happy as I used to be."

Veggie could not understand a word of it.
But Veggie knew this: there was food, there were fish, and Heidan was here to play with.

That made it the best place in the world.

zh:
细若针芒，戢戢莫知其数。

宋代淡水鱼养殖，草鱼占据了很大的一部分。宋人挖筑池塘，旁设亭台楼榭，又间或栽培莲藕、芡实、菰米等经济作物，使鱼类生长有一个良好的环境。再投入细若针芒的鱼苗，细心养育。有的鱼苗太过瘦小，难以数数，古人便插竹其间，以定分数的办法，确定容器中鱼苗的密度，来计算数量，可见宋代已有丈量鱼苗的量器。
en:
As fine as needles and packed densely, too numerous to count. 

In the Song dynasty, grass carp made up a significant portion of freshwater fish farming. People dug ponds, constructed buildings beside them, and often cultivated economic crops like lotus root, gorgon fruit, and wild rice, creating an ideal environment for fish to thrive. They would then release fry as fine as needles into the ponds and raise them with great care. Some fry were too tiny to count accurately, so the ancients inserted bamboo markers and used portioning methods to gauge the density of fry in a container. This shows that measurement tools for counting fry already existed in the Song dynasty.

zh:
天接云涛，峰来碧水。
此处百年前乃是滹沱河下游河谷，曾饱经水患摧残。后幸有历代巨子在此兴修农事水利，乃有如今十里仙峰碧水。
周显德中，前巨子鸦于此采薇舌耕，结下桃李无数。其中又以燕、鹭、隼三人最受眷重，墨家三杰之名自此鹊起。但惜白云苍狗，世事更易。洎自城中惊变，燕领巨子之责，鹭缚山水之间，隼陨九幽之下，三杰各自殊途。
只今空余碧水，不见昨日故人，逝者如斯夫。
en:
A century ago, this was the valley downstream of the Hutuo River, often ravaged by floods. Thankfully, generations of grandmasters worked here to develop farming and irrigation, shaping the beautiful stretch of peaks and waters.
During Zhou Xiande's reign, Grandmaster Raven farmed this land and mentored countless students. Among them were three standout disciples, Swallow, Heron, and Falcon, who became known as the "Three Paragons." But like ever-changing clouds, times didn't stay steady for long. After a sudden upheaval in the city, Swallow shouldered the mantle of Grandmaster, Heron was bound to peaks and rivers, and Falcon fell deep into the underworld. Each took a different path.
Now, only the clear waters remain; the faces of those old friends are gone. Such is the passing of time.

后来，纤阿女长成一位美妇人。那个少年一如既往地来总来看她。
“你说，村外的世界，是什么样子呢？”少年坐在长椅上，摇晃着腿，看着天上的圆月出神。
“村里的老人说了，我们是月亮的子民，是不能离开村子的。”纤阿女递给少年一块饼子。“这不是月亮馍，是我做的沙棘饼。”
少年接过来饼子，却没有放进嘴里，而是若有所思地盯着饼子出神。
“外面好像不太平。听说打了仗，很多人都死了。还有些人被饿死了。”
“你说，为什么只有我们可以从水里捞起月亮？明明月亮是大家的。”
“山谷外的人看着月亮，会不会也希望月亮能填饱肚子呢？”
少年的发问，让纤阿女不知道如何回答。

月华倾洒，柔和的光晕让纤阿女睁不开眼。她看到了未来的谶景——
少年在沙海里踱步，行过饿殍满地的村庄。
他如天神一般降临，朗声着歌谣，施展神迹捞起月亮。
而随后，光阴和风沙吞噬了他的少年气。手中的捞月网残破不堪，他就那么在沙海中老去，死去。
这一生，他都没有再回到月华盛极的家乡。

“不要去——”纤阿女几乎哀求地拉住少年，就像多年前哥哥拉着自己。
而少年只是挑挑眉，并没有心事被看穿的惊讶。他笑着，掰开了沙棘饼。
“阿妹手艺真好。”
en:
Later, Xian'a grew into a beautiful woman. The boy came to see her as always. 
"What is the world outside the village is like?" The boy sat on the bench, swinging his legs, gazing at the full moon in a daze. 
"The elders say we are the moon's people. We cannot leave the village." Xian'a handed the boy a flatbread. "This isn't a moon bun. It's a sea buckthorn cake I made." 
The boy took the cake but didn't eat it. Instead, he stared at it thoughtfully. 
"Outside seems troubled. I heard there's war. Many have died. Some have starved." 
"Why is it only we can scoop the moon from the water? The moon belongs to everyone." 
"When people beyond the valley look at the moon... do they also wish the moon could fill their stomachs?" 
The boy's questions left Xian'a with no answer. 

Moonlight poured down, its soft halo making it hard for Xian'a to keep her eyes open. She saw the ominous future— 
The boy pacing the sea of sand, passing villages strewn with starved bodies. 
He descended like a deity, chanting his song, performing the miracle of scooping the moon. 
And then, time and sand devoured his youthful spirit. His moon-catching net in tatters, he simply aged and died in the desert. 
In this life, he never returned to his homeland of glorious moonlight. 

"Don't go—" Xian'a almost begged, grabbing the boy's sleeve, just as her brother had held her back years ago. 
The boy just raised an eyebrow, unsurprised his thoughts were seen. He smiled and broke the sea buckthorn cake. 
"You got excellent skills."

页一

赵庄征粮，获腌肉半斤、铜钱二百文。户主藏米于地窖，掘得。

页二

一小儿跪求留粮，形似阿宝……

念起吾儿病中畏光，亦常以袖掩面。

可今若掷米，他日谁留命与阿宝……

……



页三

乱世蝼蚁，惟附强军得活！

病弱孺子，须恃父功求生！

……

人人求活，吾儿……亦求活。



页四

缴粟……记一分功勋……

纳财……争一日归期……



页五

于郊野斩十人有余，因立功得假一日。

疾奔归家，全村荒凉。

锁锈，灶冷……吾儿阿宝……何处？

寻遍未果，无奈返回。

幸得一同僚悄语相告：得杜大人恩，阿宝已至他处养病。

附以乳齿一颗为凭。乳齿细小，齿根带血。

……

阿宝……正当龀年……

……

积年煎熬痛楚，尽化此粒雪齿间。

忽……见掌中漫天飞雪，雪中得见阿宝……

儿在彼处，吾自当奋进……

……

威！威！威！



页六

杀……杀……杀……

威……威……威……
en:
Page One

Grain levy at Zhao Hamlet. Took half a jin of cured meat and two hundred copper coins.
The householder had hidden grain in the cellar. Dug it up.

Pressed Li Village for military tax. Took two live chickens and several iron tools.

Intercepted a band of refugees in the wilds. Took three able-bodied men into camp.
Confiscated a pair of hidden silver bracelets and two sacks of grain.



Page Two

A small child knelt and begged to keep the grain. Looked like Bao...

I remembered how my own boy, when he was ill, feared the light and would hide his face in his sleeve.

But if I let this grain go now, who will leave Bao a way to live another day...

...



Page Three

In troubled times, ants and insects live only by clinging to a strong army.

A sickly child lives only by his father's merit.

...

Everyone struggles to live. My son... he too struggles to live.



Page Four

Turn in grain... one mark of merit entered...

Offer up wealth... gain one more day's leave to go home...



Page Five

I killed more than ten men in the outskirts, and for that merit was granted one day's leave.

I raced home without stopping, only to find the whole village desolate.

The lock was rusted. The stove was cold...
My son Bao... where was he?

I searched everywhere and found nothing. In the end, I had no choice but to turn back.

By good fortune, a fellow soldier quietly told me that by Lord Du's grace, Bao had been sent elsewhere to recover.

He gave me a milk tooth as proof. It was tiny, with blood still at the root.

...

Bao... was only just at the age of losing his milk teeth...

...

All the torment and bitterness of these years seemed to gather in that single white tooth.

Then... suddenly, it was as if my palm were filled with snow, and there in the snow I saw Bao...

If my boy is there, then I must press on...

...

Might! Might! Might!



Page Six

Kill... kill... kill...

Might... might... might...
Fen Shang

zh: 滹沱河南岸，有一沙洲，名曰荻花。盖因秋风起时，荻芦惊风，飞花如雪。洲上多雾，晨昏之间，水气腾起，故常有行旅夜泊之客，失路于芦荻深处。或可闻雾中清歌袅袅，声若在旁。顺歌而行，竟可脱出迷津。自此有芦中仙子之说，言伊人渡水而来，引迷途者溯游归乡。然今岁寒重，滹沱河冻，虏骑作乱，乡人尽南下避祸，再未听得江上歌声。今逢四海为家日，故垒萧萧芦荻秋。
en: Upon the South Hutuo Bank, there lies a shoal named Reed Flower. When the autumn gales rise, the reeds sway in the wind, their white tufts drifting like a flurry of snow. Enshrouded in mist, the shoal breathes forth vapors at dawn and dusk. Many travelers, mooring their boat by night, become ensnared within the labyrinth of reeds. At times, an ethereal song wafts through the fog, sounding so near it brushes the ear. Following the strain, one may find deliverance from the misty maze. Thus grew the legend of the Reed Fairy, a lady who drifts across the waters to guide the lost back to their ancestral homes. But this year, the frost bites deep, and Hutuo River is locked in ice. Due to the marauders, the folk have fled south for sanctuary, and the song upon the river is heard no more. Now, as we drift homeless across the realm, only the soughing reeds remain by the desolate ramparts in the autumn chill.

闻说往昔此处不似今时，尝有精怪之传言，然皆口耳之谈，渺不可考。山间昼夜景致殊异，入夜后游人仍众，多为乘月攀岭之士，故虽深宵犹见喧阗。山巅有九幽石碑一座，后因文津馆之故，似曾移其位。

攀山途中，景致层出，颇可玩赏。沿途多见摩崖石刻，或镌诗文，或勒箴言，刀法刚劲，笔力沉雄。经年风雨剥蚀，更显苍苔斑驳，古意盎然。另有五大夫松虬枝探云，登高必自碑寂然独立，皆承载旧闻轶事，足供行人驻足品读。山间偶有清涧细流，潺湲泻玉，涉之可涤尘虑，亦添游趣。

何人至此，及登顶极目，但见云海翻澜，朝暾流金，顿觉豪情盈怀，天地入抱，果有“一览众山小”之慨。
en:
Isle of Mount Tai borders the sea, gazing across the waters toward Qinghe. Upon disembarking at the pier, one is greeted by several households nestled against the mountain. They sell local rustic fare, among which is a century-old dumpling shop where the hearths never cool. This place is known as Cloudside Village.
Rumor has it that in ages past, this land was unlike it is today. Tales of wandering spirits and monsters once circulated, yet these are mere whispers passed from mouth to ear, impossible to verify. The mountain presents vastly different vistas between day and night. Even after dusk, travelers remain plentiful. Most are scholars ascending the ridges under the moonlight, making the deep night as bustling as the day. At the summit once stood the Nine Hells Stele. It seems to have been relocated later, perhaps due to the affairs of the Inkbound Order.
The journey up the mountain offers an endless array of wondrous sights. Along the path, cliffside carvings are abundant: some engrave poetry, others bear words of wisdom. The chisel strokes are vigorous, the calligraphy profound and bold. Weathered by years of wind and rain, the mottled green moss only deepens their venerable, ancient charm. Furthermore, the Wudafu Pine stretches its gnarled branches toward the clouds, and the Ascent Stele's Origin stands in solemn solitude. Each bears the weight of forgotten anecdotes, giving travelers ample reason to pause and ponder. Occasionally, clear streams and cascading springs spill like liquid jade. Wading through them washes away mortal anxieties and adds joy to the wandering soul.
Whoever comes here and climbs to the summit will see a churning sea of clouds and the morning sun pouring out molten gold. In that instant, the heart swells with exhilaration, as if heaven and earth could be taken into one's embrace, and one finally understands the feeling behind the line: all the other mountains seem small at a single glance.

zh:
头领狗是这片地方的狗中老大。大家狗服它，不仅是因为它打架厉害，还因为它是个仁义的好狗。

这附近的狗崽子，捡！走不动道的流浪狗，也捡！
自己抢来的第一口肉，先撕下来给最老的那只。
夜里风大，它就趴在最外圈，让小崽子们全挤在它肚皮下面。

所以头领狗很忙。它得看地盘，得找吃的。它也很累。伤疤一层压一层，老伤没好，新伤又添。

可只要有空，它还是会一只一只地教小崽子们。
教胆子小的，遇见人别先夹尾巴，教爱冲的，咬之前先看清对面是谁。
教它们怎么分食、不闹，怎么在桥下躲雨，在风里找到回家的路。

偶尔，它也会亲自上场。
一声低吼，狗群瞬间让出空地。头领压低身体，示范怎么扑、怎么闪、怎么护喉。
小崽子们学会了，蜂拥而上，往它身上扑，然后吵吵闹闹汪成一大团。

这是头领狗每每想起来，最开心的时候。
en:
Alpha is the leader of the dogs in this area. The other dogs respect him not just because he's a great fighter, but because he's a righteous and kind dog.

Lost puppies in the neighborhood? Rescue them! Strays too old to walk? Rescue them too!
The first bite of meat he scavenges is always torn off for the oldest dog.
When the wind is strong at night, he lies on the outermost circle, letting the puppies huddle under his belly.

So Alpha is very busy. He has to watch the territory and find food. He is also very tired. Scars are layered upon one another; new wounds are added before the old ones heal.

But whenever he has a spare moment, he still teaches the puppies one by one.
He teaches the timid ones not to tuck their tails between their legs when they meet humans, and the impulsive ones to see who they're facing before they bite.
He teaches them how to share food without fighting, how to take shelter from the rain under the bridge, and how to find the way home in the wind.

Occasionally, he joins in himself.
With a low growl, the pack instantly clears a space. Alpha lowers his body, demonstrating how to pounce, dodge, and protect the throat.
The puppies learn and swarm over him, barking and tumbling into a big, noisy heap.

Thinking back on it, these are always Alpha's happiest moments.

zh: 《孟子》成书于战国中后期，孟子及其弟子所纂。《汉书·艺文志》著录十一篇，今存七篇，每篇分上下，共十四卷，三万五千余言。内容记孟子与诸家辩争、教诲弟子、游说诸侯等事。其论说以性善论为发端，倡仁政，首提民贵君轻。至中唐，韩愈推孟轲为先秦得孔子真传之唯一。
en: Completed in the mid-to-late Warring States period, Mencius was compiled by the philosopher himself alongside his disciples. The Book of Han: Treatise on Literature originally recorded eleven chapters, but only seven survive today. Each chapter is divided into upper and lower parts, totaling fourteen volumes and over thirty-five thousand words. The contents chronicle Mencius's spirited debates with rival schools, his teachings to his followers, and his attempts to lobby feudal lords. His discourses are rooted in the theory of innate human goodness, advocating for benevolent governance, and famously declaring that the people are of supreme importance, while the sovereign is of least consequence. By the mid-Tang dynasty, the scholar Han Yu elevated Mencius as the sole authentic inheritor of Confucius's teachings from the pre-Qin era.

zh:
【祭法第二十三】

祭法：有虞氏禘黄帝而郊喾，祖颛顼而宗尧。夏后氏亦禘黄帝而郊鲧，祖颛顼而宗禹。殷人禘喾而郊冥，祖契而宗汤。周人禘喾而郊稷，祖文王而宗武王。
燔柴于泰坛，祭天也；瘗埋于泰折，祭地也；用骍犊。埋少牢于泰昭，祭时也；相近于坎坛，祭寒暑也。王宫，祭日也；夜明，祭月也；幽宗，祭星也；雩宗，祭水旱也；四坎坛，祭四时也。山林、川谷、丘陵，能出云为风雨，见怪物，皆曰神。有天下者，祭百神。诸侯在其地则祭之，亡其地则不祭。
大凡生于天地之间者，皆曰命。其万物死，皆曰折；人死，曰鬼；此五代之所不变也。七代之所以更立者：禘、郊、宗、祖；其余不变也。
天下有王，分地建国，置都立邑，设庙祧坛墠而祭之，乃为亲疏多少之数。是故：王立七庙，一坛一墠，曰考庙，曰王考庙，曰皇考庙，曰显考庙，曰祖考庙；皆月祭之。远庙为祧，有二祧，享尝乃止。去祧为坛，去坛为墠。坛墠，有祷焉祭之，无祷乃止。去墠曰鬼。诸侯立五庙，一坛一墠。曰考庙，曰王考庙，曰皇考庙，皆月祭之；显考庙，祖考庙，享尝乃止。去祖为坛，去坛为墠。坛墠，有祷焉祭之，无祷乃止。去墠为鬼。大夫立三庙二坛，曰考庙，曰王考庙，曰皇考庙，享尝乃止。显考祖考无庙，有祷焉，为坛祭之。去坛为鬼。适士二庙一坛，曰考庙，曰王考庙，享尝乃止。皇考无庙，有祷焉，为坛祭之。去坛为鬼。官师一庙，曰考庙。王考无庙而祭之，去王考曰鬼。庶士庶人无庙，死曰鬼。
……
en:
【Sacrificial Rites XXIII】

The sacrificial rites: The Yu clan offered the Di sacrifice to the Yellow Emperor and the Jiao sacrifice to Ku, honoring Zhuanxu as ancestor and Yao as patriarch. The Xia dynasty likewise offered the Di sacrifice to the Yellow Emperor and the Jiao sacrifice to Gun, honoring Zhuanxu as ancestor and Yu as patriarch. The Yin people offered the Di sacrifice to Ku and the Jiao sacrifice to Ming, honoring Xie as ancestor and Tang as patriarch. The Zhou people offered the Di sacrifice to Ku and the Jiao sacrifice to Ji, honoring King Wen as ancestor and King Wu as patriarch.
They burned offerings on the Great Altar to sacrifice to Heaven; they buried offerings at the Great Mound to sacrifice to Earth, using a red calf. They buried a lesser offering at the Great Shrine to sacrifice to the seasons; they made offerings at the pits and altars to sacrifice to cold and heat. The Royal Palace was for sacrificing to the Sun; the Night Light was for sacrificing to the Moon; the Dark Shrine was for sacrificing to the Stars; the Rain Shrine was for sacrificing to water and drought; the four pits and altars were for sacrificing to the four seasons. Mountains, forests, rivers, valleys, and hills—those that could produce clouds and bring wind and rain, or manifest strange phenomena, were all called spirits. Those who possessed the realm sacrificed to all spirits. Feudal lords sacrificed to those within their own territories; if they lost their territories, they did not sacrifice.
Generally, all things born between Heaven and Earth are called "destined." When all creatures die, it is called "breaking"; when humans die, it is called "ghost." This has remained unchanged through five dynasties. What the seven dynasties changed were the Di, Jiao, ancestral, and patriarchal sacrifices; the rest remained unchanged.
When there is a king in the realm, he divides the land and establishes states, sets up capitals and cities, and establishes temples, shrines, altars, and mounds for sacrifice, thereby determining the degrees of closeness and distance and the numbers of offerings. Therefore: The king established seven temples—one altar and one mound—namely, the Temple of the Deceased Father, the Temple of the Grandfather, the Temple of the Great-Grandfather, the Temple of the Illustrious Forefather, and the Temple of the Ancestral Forefather; all were sacrificed to monthly. Temples farther removed were called "tiao," and there were two tiao, where seasonal offerings were made only. Beyond the tiao was the altar; beyond the altar was the mound. At altars and mounds, sacrifices were made when there were prayers; when there were no prayers, they ceased. Beyond the mound, they were called "ghosts." Feudal lords established five temples—one altar and one mound—namely, the Temple of the Deceased Father, the Temple of the Grandfather, and the Temple of the Great-Grandfather, all sacrificed to monthly; the Temple of the Illustrious Forefather and the Temple of the Ancestral Forefather received only seasonal offerings. Beyond the ancestral temple was the altar; beyond the altar was the mound. At altars and mounds, sacrifices were made when there were prayers; when there were no prayers, they ceased. Beyond the mound, they were called "ghosts." Great officers established three temples and two altars—namely, the Temple of the Deceased Father, the Temple of the Grandfather, and the Temple of the Great-Grandfather, receiving only seasonal offerings. The Illustrious Forefather and the Ancestral Forefather had no temples; when there were prayers, altars were made for sacrifice. Beyond the altar, they were called "ghosts." Regular officers had two temples and one altar—namely, the Temple of the Deceased Father and the Temple of the Grandfather, receiving only seasonal offerings. The Great-Grandfather had no temple; when there were prayers, an altar was made for sacrifice. Beyond the altar, they were called "ghosts." Minor officers had one temple—namely, the Temple of the Deceased Father. The Grandfather had no temple but was sacrificed to; beyond the Grandfather, they were called "ghosts." Common officers and common people had no temples; at death, they were called "ghosts."
……

en: Early symptoms are headache, low-grade fever, tiredness, and loss of appetite. Even after a bite or scratch has healed, you might feel pain, numbness, or tingling where you were hurt. Within two to three days, the person can become restless and easily agitated, and may develop a fear of water, wind, or bright light. Just seeing or feeling these things can trigger throat spasms or even full-body convulsions. In the final stage, the patient often becomes calm and the spasms stop, but serious problems set in—paralysis, weak muscles, lost reflexes, dilated pupils, trouble breathing, and heart failure. This phase is extremely dangerous and usually ends in death from respiratory failure within about eight days.

后来你长大了，那把小剑不再适合你，连同剑穗也被你逐渐遗忘。
直至今日再见，你才发现，原来此物一直被人悉心收着，只因旧居荒废而积满灰尘。
许是因为眷念之情从未被岁月斩断，百转千回后，它终究又归于你手中。
en:
When you were young, you were captivated by the tassels on the sword hilts of martial artists, and pestered Uncle Jiang for one. But he ignored you as if he hadn't heard. 
During sword practice, you'd stare blankly at the bare pommel, your mind filled with images of swaying tassels. Uncle Jiang would say with a stern face, "Your swordsmanship is lacking, yet you fixate on such trivialities." 
He punished you with a thousand practice swings, lasting until the sun set. That day, you didn't even have the spirit to sulk and fell straight asleep. 
The next morning, you were astonished to find a brand new tassel tied to the pommel by an unknown hand. Overjoyed, you showed it off everywhere. 
As you grew older, that small sword no longer suited you, and along with it, the tassel faded from memory. 
Only upon seeing it again today did you realize someone had treasured it all along, letting it gather dust only as the old residence fell into disrepair. 
Perhaps because the longing was never severed by time, after countless twists and turns, it finally returned to your hands.
This stolen fire could boil the tide.

zh:
【三更天】
其实三更天的钱我一早就在赚。有个三更天的阎王是我的老主顾：她找我打听人，我就去跑一趟，踩踩点。今天她又找我，我就忍不住跟她倒苦水，说我点子真背，在别人身上一文钱都捞不着，还是你们好，肯给钱。
噢，她还给我带酥饼吃。
但这么一说，她又开始跟我念叨她那套“渡人”的屁话，说什么这世道里活着就是受罪，早死早超生啥啥的。
虽然我是啃着她买的饼，但我还是说，她这就是放屁。活着不好吗？活着才有酥饼吃啊！照这么说，我也过得够惨了，你咋不顺手把我也渡了？
谁知道这阎王还真说可以！说她刀很快，保证走的时候啥感觉没有。
哇！老子火一下就上来了，这疯子！我就说这买卖不干了，她居然说“那便寻他人”。
好家伙，真绝情，我还当咱俩有点交情呢！
但是走之前，她又问我酥饼好不好吃。我说好吃。她说下次还给我带这家。
……生意都黄了，哪来的下次？真搞不懂这群疯子想的什么。

【墨山道】
今天翻垃圾，不对，翻废仓库的时候，想看看有啥能顺的，正好撞见一个小妮，捡了一堆木头。
我一打眼就知道她是墨山道的。虽然她使劲摇头不承认，但看她连木头都当宝贝，估计也榨不出油水。算了算了。

【文津馆】
我一直有点怵文津馆的人，这回果然也一样。我今天硬着头皮进翰林院溜达，见文津馆的人都在那儿写写画画，嘴里叽里咕噜的，我一个字都听不懂。我站那儿跟个傻子一样，浑身不自在。
刚想开溜，被个小哥叫住了。我心说坏了，这是要赶我呢？
结果，他塞了我俩包子，还给了十文钱，说看我晃半天了，有难处就找门口弟子说一声。
包子不好吃，干巴巴的，一点没味。不过毕竟白拿的嘛。文津馆这帮人还蛮好的。
en:
[Midnight Blades] 
To be honest, I've actually been earning from the Midnight Blades folk for a while. There's a living Yama who comes to me often: she asks for information, and I scout around for her. Today she came again, and I couldn't help complaining—everywhere else I make nothing, but at least she pays. 
She even brought pastries for me. 
But once she starts, she always returns to her talk about "saving souls"—how living is nothing but suffering, how early death means early release, and so on. 
I was eating the pastries she bought, but I still told her she was talking nonsense. What's wrong with living? If you're alive, you get to eat pastries. If that's her logic, my life has been miserable enough—why not "save" me as well? 
To my astonishment, she said she could. Her blade was quick, she said, and I wouldn't feel a thing. 
That startled me so much I lost my temper. I told her I wanted no part in that kind of work anymore. She simply replied, "Then I will seek someone else." 
So heartless—I truly thought we had at least a little friendship! 
Yet before she left, she still asked whether the pastries were good. I said yes. She said she would bring more next time. 
...But with the job already fallen through, what "next time" could there possibly be?
I really cannot understand what goes on in these people's minds. 

[Mohist Hill] 
Today, while searching through some discarded items—or rather, an old warehouse—I was hoping to find something useful when I happened upon a young girl collecting a pile of wood. 
I could tell right away she was from the Mohist Hill. Yet she shook her head firmly to deny it. Seeing how she treated even scraps of wood like precious belongings, I figured there was no real profit to be made from her. Oh well, no matter. 

[The Inkbound Order] 
I've always felt a bit intimidated by those at the Inkbound Order, and today was no different. I nervously wandered into the Hanlin Academy, where the scholars at the Inkbound Order were busy writing and painting, mumbling in a language I couldn't understand at all. I just stood there feeling completely out of place and awkward. 
Just as I was about to leave, a young scholar called out to me. I thought I was about to be told to move on. 
Instead, he handed me two steamed buns and ten coins, saying he noticed I'd been hanging around for a while and if I ever had trouble, I should talk to one of the disciples by the gate. 
The buns weren't very tasty—dry and bland—but free food is always welcome. The Inkbound Order guys are actually quite kind.

I took you for a good person.

And yet, Unhappy grew all the same into a lively, spirited cat. The summer solstice brings three signs in turn: first, the antlers of the deer begin to shed; second, the cicadas start their song; and third, the crow-dipper herb sprouts forth. It made its home and raised its family near the post station where foreign travelers gathered, fathering many kittens of its own. It was forever curious, sniffing about this way and that, searching among the strange and varied goods for the scent of some foreign rat. It often thought that perhaps, one day, it too might cross the seas, and see with its own eyes all manner of strange creatures: the gaudy dragonflies, the kitchen crickets, the tiny biting gnats, and the weaving-lady spiders...

en: Historically known as the Le Family Jujube, Qi Jujube, or Qingzhou Golden Silk Jujube, it is affectionately called the "beautiful little jujube" by locals. The ancient agricultural text, Agrarian Codex, notes: "Qingzhou produces the Le Family Jujube. Plump in flesh and tiny in pit, it is rich and luscious, ranking first under heaven. Village elders pass down the tale that when General Yue Yi conquered the State of Qi, he brought the seeds from the State of Yan." The great poet Su Shi also praised it in his Dongpo’s Records: "The Qi Jujube is sweet without being cloying, nourishing the spleen and replenishing vitality. Travelers carry it on long journeys as a perfect substitute for dry rations." Such accounts testify to its prized status.

zh:
【礼器第十】

礼器是故大备。大备，盛德也。礼释回，增美质。措则正，施则行。其在人也，如竹箭之有筠也，如松柏之有心也。二者居天下之大端矣，故贯四时而不改柯易叶。故君子有礼，则外谐而内无怨，故物无不怀仁，鬼神飨德。
先王之立礼也，有本有文。忠信，礼之本也；义理，礼之文也。无本不立，无文不行。礼也者，合于天时，设于地财，顺于鬼神，合于人心，理万物者也。是故天时有生也，地理有宜也，人官有能也，物曲有利也。故天不生，地不养，君子不以为礼，鬼神弗飨也。居山以鱼鳖为礼，居泽以鹿豕为礼，君子谓之不知礼。故必举其定国之数，以为礼之大经。礼之大伦，以地广狭；礼之薄厚，与年之上下。是故年虽大杀，众不匡惧，则上之制礼也节矣。
礼，时为大，顺次之，体次之，宜次之，称次之。尧授舜，舜授禹，汤放桀，武王伐纣，时也。互注。诗云：匪革其犹，聿追来孝。
天地之祭，宗庙之事，父子之道，君臣之义，伦也。
社稷山川之事，鬼神之祭，体也。
丧祭之用，宾客之交，义也。
羔豚而祭，百官皆足；大牢而祭，不必有余，此之谓称也。诸侯以龟为宝，以圭为瑞。家不宝龟，不藏圭，不台门，言有称也。
礼有以多为贵者，天子七庙，诸侯五，大夫三，士一，天子之豆二十有六，诸公十有六，诸侯十有二，上大夫八，下大夫六。诸侯七介七牢，大夫五介五牢。天子之席五重，诸侯之席三重，大夫再重。天子崩，七月而葬，五重八翣；诸侯五月而葬，三重六翣；大夫三月而葬，再重四翣。此以多为贵也。
有以少为贵者，天子无介，祭天特牲。天子适诸侯，诸侯膳以犊。诸侯相朝，灌用郁鬯，无笾豆之荐。大夫聘礼以脯醢。天子一食，诸侯再，大夫士三，食力无数。大路繁缨一就，次路繁缨七就。圭璋特，琥璜爵，鬼神之祭单席。诸侯视朝，大夫特，士旅之。此以少为贵也。
有以大为贵者，宫室之量，器皿之度，棺椁之厚，丘封之大，此以大为贵也。
有以小为贵者，宗庙之祭，贵者献以爵，贱者献以散，尊者举觯，卑者举角。五献之尊，门外缶，门内壶，君尊瓦甒，此以小为贵也。
有以高为贵者，天子之堂九尺，诸侯七尺，大夫五尺，士三尺，天子诸侯台门。此以高为贵也。
……
en:
【Ritual Vessels X】

Ritual vessels are therefore greatly complete. Great completeness is abundant virtue. Ritual releases from what is crooked and enhances the beauty of substance. When applied, it makes things correct; when practiced, it makes them proceed. In a person, it is like the bamboo's glossy exterior, like the pine and cypress's heart. These two occupy the great foundations of the world, thus they pass through the four seasons without changing their branches or leaves. Therefore, when a gentleman has ritual, he is harmonious without and without resentment within, so all things cherish benevolence, and ghosts and spirits enjoy his virtue.
When the former kings established ritual, it had both substance and form. Loyalty and trustworthiness are the substance of ritual; righteousness and principle are its form. Without substance, it cannot stand; without form, it cannot be practiced. Ritual is that which accords with the seasons of heaven, is set up according to the resources of earth, follows the ghosts and spirits, conforms to the human heart, and regulates all things. Therefore, what heaven produces in season, what geography makes suitable, what human faculties are capable of, and what things bend to benefit—these are all considered. Thus, what heaven does not produce and earth does not nurture, the gentleman does not use for ritual, and ghosts and spirits do not enjoy. Dwelling in the mountains and using fish and turtles for ritual, or dwelling in the marshes and using deer and boars for ritual, the gentleman calls this ignorance of ritual. Therefore, one must take the fixed resources of one's state as the great standard of ritual. The great principle of ritual is according to the breadth of the land; the thickness or thinness of ritual is according to the abundance or scarcity of the year. Therefore, even if the year brings great famine, the people do not fear, for the superior's regulation of ritual is measured.
In ritual, timeliness is the greatest, following is next, substance is next, appropriateness is next, and proportion is next. Yao yielded to Shun, Shun yielded to Yu, Tang banished Jie, and King Wu attacked Zhou—these were matters of timeliness. Mutual annotations. Shiyun says: Not to change their plans, but to pursue filial piety from the past.
The sacrifices to heaven and earth, the affairs of the ancestral temple, the way of father and son, the righteousness of ruler and minister—these are matters of order.
The affairs of altars of soil and grain, mountains and rivers, and the sacrifices to ghosts and spirits—these are matters of substance.
The expenses of mourning and sacrifice, and the interactions of guests—these are matters of appropriateness.
Sacrificing with lambs and piglets, all the officers are satisfied; sacrificing with the great offering, there need not be surplus—this is called proportion. The feudal lords treasure the tortoise and regard the gui jade as auspicious. A noble family does not treasure the tortoise, does not store the gui, and does not have a terrace gate—this is said to have proportion.
There are cases where more is valued in ritual: the Son of Heaven has seven temples, the feudal lords five, the great officers three, the officers one; the Son of Heaven's dishes number twenty-six, the dukes sixteen, the feudal lords twelve, the high great officers eight, the lower great officers six. The feudal lords have seven attendants and seven offerings of cattle; the great officers have five attendants and five offerings. The Son of Heaven's mat is five layers, the feudal lords' mats are three layers, the great officers' two layers. When the Son of Heaven dies, he is buried after seven months, with five layers and eight feather fans; the feudal lords are buried after five months, with three layers and six feather fans; the great officers are buried after three months, with two layers and four feather fans. This is valuing more.
There are cases where less is valued: the Son of Heaven has no attendant, and in sacrificing to heaven uses a single victim. When the Son of Heaven visits the feudal lords, the feudal lords offer him a calf. When feudal lords meet each other, they pour fragrant wine, without the presentation of bamboo baskets and wooden platters. In the great officer's mission of inquiry, dried meat and minced meat are used. The Son of Heaven eats one mouthful, the feudal lords two, the great officers and officers three, and those who labor by eating have no number. The great carriage has one tassel of ornaments, the secondary carriage has seven tassels. The gui and zhang jades are presented alone; the hu and huang jades accompany the drinking cup; in the sacrifices to ghosts and spirits, a single mat is used. When the feudal lords hold court, the great officers are received singly, the officers in groups. This is valuing less.
There are cases where greatness is valued: the size of palaces and chambers, the measure of vessels and utensils, the thickness of inner and outer coffins, the magnitude of mounds and tombs—this is valuing greatness.
There are cases where smallness is valued: in the sacrifices of the ancestral temple, the noble offer with the jue cup, the humble offer with the san cup; the exalted raise the zhi cup, the lowly raise the jiao cup. In the five-offering feast, outside the gate is the fou jar, inside the gate is the hu pot, and the lord's vessel is the clay wu—this is valuing smallness.
There are cases where height is valued: the Son of Heaven's hall is nine feet, the feudal lords' seven feet, the great officers' five feet, the officers' three feet; the Son of Heaven and feudal lords have terrace gates. This is valuing height.
……

zh:
玉米、土豆、胡萝卜、番茄、辣椒等作物，原本不产于中国，经对外贸易交流，引入中国进行广泛栽种。这些作物传入后，大幅提升了粮食产量，亦有榨油、制糖、酿造、调味等多种用途，很快便有了广泛的历史记载和重要的民间地位。
由于这类作物在历史中的重要地位，十六巷选择了这些作物作为可产出的家园原料，实际是早于其在历史上真实出现的年代的。
en:
Crops such as corn, potatoes, carrots, tomatoes, and peppers were not originally produced in China. They were introduced to China through foreign trade and widely cultivated. After their introduction, these crops greatly increased grain production and had multiple uses such as oil extraction, sugar making, brewing, and seasoning. They soon had extensive historical records and an important folk status. 
Due to the important historical status of such crops, Sixteen Lanes selected them as producible homestead materials, which is actually earlier than their actual historical appearance.

I am Jingxuan, Abbot of Reflection Temple.
Recently, a multitude of refugees have sought shelter in our temple, fleeing the disaster in Jinghu. Upon arrival, several already suffered from relentless fever, coughing up blood, and bearing red rashes on their flesh.
Yet our temple has neither healers nor medicine, and the sick continue to grow in number. My strength is spent. I fear once the plague fully erupts, the living will perish, and the dead will find no peace.
I send my eldest disciple into the city with this letter, begging your clinic to dispatch a healer or two with medicine to our temple. If you cannot come, please grant us a prescription and herbs, so I may attempt to save them.
The temple is impoverished, but we will offer what meager incense money we have in return. I beg the benevolent ones to take pity on these wandering souls of our chaotic times, and grant us your aid swiftly.
